articles.title: How Iran Changed War
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
MICHAEL C. HOROWITZ is Senior Fellow for Technology and Innovation at the Council on Foreign Relations and Richard Perry Professor and Director of the Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania. From 2022 to 2024, he served as U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Force Development and Emerging Capabilities.
When the United States began bombing Iran, it expected to quickly overwhelm the country’s government. In the war’s first 24 hours, American and Israeli forces hit roughly 1,000 targets. Over the following 37 days, they blew up 12,000 more, laying waste to much of Iran’s military infrastructure. The strikes killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, Iran’s minister of defense, and the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But more than six months later, the Iranian regime not only remains intact; it is perhaps stronger than before. It immediately replaced lost officials and struck back at Washington and its regional partners. And it shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, driving up energy prices around the world and winning newfound political leverage—all to the great frustration of U.S. officials.
There are several reasons why Iran performed surprisingly well. For one, the country had long planned for American and Israeli attacks, so it was prepared to reconstitute its government when top leaders were killed. It was also able to import enough goods to keep its economy from completely collapsing despite a U.S. naval blockade. But one of the most significant factors is that the Islamic Republic had built up a large arsenal of cheap yet accurate drones and missiles. These munitions made Iran’s counterattacks effective and allowed it to close the strait—and thus deter American escalation.
In doing so, Iran has demonstrated something broader. The age of what I called precise mass—or high-volume, low-cost, precision-guided weapons—is well underway. It is no longer possible for the U.S. military, or any military, to win a full-blown war simply by using small numbers of exquisite weapons to dazzle opponents. Weaker countries can match stronger ones through offensive barrages. Offense is currently cheaper than defense: the price of effective interceptors has yet to fall to the level of attack drones and missiles, which means defending against precise mass is extremely costly. After all, militaries cannot endlessly block salvos of $35,000 Shahed-136 attack drones with $4 million Patriot missiles.
To be sure, the war in Iran also shows that advanced technology remains essential. The United States, for example, had great success hitting valuable Iranian sites because it has artificial intelligence systems that can identify and recommend targets faster than ever before. American exquisite weapons are still much harder to stop than cheaper ones, and they are more likely to destroy targets in a single strike. But the world is learning from Iran, building on what Ukraine had already made clear: the future of war lies in part in precise mass. Everyone will now embrace the imperative of producing and using hosts of cheap and disposable weapons systems, changing warfare and the military balance.
In war, it might seem as if wealthy states always benefit from new military capabilities. But the reality is more complicated. If a new system is expensive, it indeed favors rich incumbents. But if it is cheap and demands large organizational changes to adopt, other countries can take advantage just as quickly—if not faster. In fact, the most powerful militaries in the world often struggle in the face of required disruptive organizational change, as their prior success has created bureaucracies and organizational biases that make adaption harder. As a result, they have a hard time integrating new capabilities that cannot be plugged into their existing structures.
Precise mass is just such a capability. The most conventionally powerful militaries are organized around small numbers of exquisite, expensive, hard-to-produce weapons and platforms such as Tomahawk missiles and F-35s. Their units train and plan around these systems. They thus cannot easily adjust to precise mass capabilities, which require different kinds of training and entirely new conceptions of how to fight. Exquisite systems, for instance, are scarce, so units must take great care not to waste systems and to minimize the risk of destruction. With precise mass, by contrast, units are supposed to move quickly and not make the perfect the enemy of the good. This helps explain why the United States has struggled to adapt to precise mass—even though the country invented precision guidance and boasts the best military in the world.
Iran, meanwhile, has been broadly locked out of some more advanced military capabilities. As a result, it had to invest heavily in long-range, one-way attack systems and cheap ballistic missiles. The result is a war where Iran has dramatically outperformed expectations. Tehran could not go blow-for-blow with the U.S. military’s exquisite weapons, but it did not need to, because it could rapidly fire relatively accurate drones and cheap missiles at U.S. bases and the region’s critical infrastructure. The United States has dealt billions of dollars of damage to Iran in turn, but only by burning through its stockpiles of Tomahawks, SM-6 missiles, and other expensive systems. As a result, Washington now has to sprint to resupply its own stocks and those of partners elsewhere, such as Taiwan and Ukraine.
Thanks to rigorous preparations, meanwhile, Tehran has been able to withstand the intensive damage. In the years before the war, Iran built a vast underground network of missile infrastructure spread across its territory that has proved impossible for U.S. and Israeli forces to eliminate thus far. The United States had even more trouble destroying Iran’s heavily dispersed missile production facilities, inverting assumptions that have guided American airpower campaigns since Operation Desert Storm against Iraq in 1991, where the emphasis was destroying existing weapons stockpiles.
Iran has shown that weaker states are no longer priced out of the military power game, and the United States has discovered that stronger states are not guaranteed the upper hand in major battles. Little wonder, then, that countries rich and poor are investing in precise mass. North Korea, for example, has received Iran’s Shahed technology and production equipment from Russia and is using it to develop its own cheap uncrewed vehicles. A company in Nigeria has contracted with a Turkish manufacturer to build 100,000 one-way attack drones at local assembly facilities. Poland has increased spending on drones and counterdrone systems from about $27 million in late 2023 to roughly $6.9 billion this year and established domestic drone factories. Six European states, including France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a one-way attack drone with a range of over 300 miles and a target cost of less than $100,000. Saudi Arabia has unveiled its own attack drone modeled on the Shahed with a supposed range of more than 900 miles. And Japan’s governing party has requested a record $55.6 billion defense budget, largely so that it can buy great quantities of attack drones.
The Iran war shows that nearly every military can acquire lots of precision strike weapons that cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece. But defense remains much more expensive. There are very few reliable interceptors that cost less than $1 million. To repel Iran’s precise mass, Washington had to use about 65 percent of its Patriot interceptors and 35 percent of its THAAD interceptors, leaving it with roughly 1,000 and 250 of each type, respectively. The country’s partners in the Middle East are also running out of air defenses.
For the United States, this challenge was inevitable. The exclusive focus on exquisite systems since the end of the Cold War extended to how it approached defense, emphasizing antimissile systems intended to stop high-end ballistic and cruise missile attacks. Meanwhile, policymakers assumed that wars would be short, so they did not focus on designing defenses that could be easily scaled.
Now, Washington and other governments are trying to come up with cheaper defensive systems, experimenting with technologies such as directed energy weapons and high-power microwave systems that could destroy incoming drones. They are looking at interceptor systems that simply need to get near drones and explode to destroy them, rather than actually make contact head on. The international market has started to move: Ukraine is fielding interceptor drones that cost just $1,400 apiece, and European and Gulf-based startups are likewise building cheaper interceptors. But none of these systems appears ready to scale now.
The Iran war has also highlighted American capabilities that should prove useful in the new era of warfare. Over the last few years, AI that aggregates intelligence from many sources and cues up targeting recommendations for commanders has become an essential part of conflict, giving the United States—with its many AI companies and experience building so-called decision-support platforms—an advantage. Washington, for example, fielded the Maven Smart System, allowing it to dramatically increase the rate of its military strikes. This system has not been flawless; it may, for example, have mistakenly flagged an Iranian school as a target due to faulty intelligence inputs it was not enabled to check, contributing to a strike that killed over 100 children. The incredible speed of targeting selection also increases the risk of automation bias, whereby humans will outsource cognition to imperfect algorithms, leading to errors. But the system has apparently made targeting relatively more accurate, and the U.S. military can implement reforms that would make targeting mistakes even less likely. That means the binding constraint on how quickly a U.S. campaign could move is no longer intelligence processing, but inventory.
Critically, however, Washington’s AI gains came from better data architecture and the organizational integration of models mostly unveiled in 2025 or earlier, not the latest frontier ones. That means the current race to artificial general intelligence is not the principal driver of how AI is shaping warfare. In fact, as cheap open-source models inevitably gain the same capabilities as the ones Washington is using today, other militaries will find it easier to use AI to build similar decision-support tools. That may include Iran’s, which according to the AI company Anthropic tried to use its large language model Claude to target U.S. forces in the region.
The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran shows that the age of precise mass is here. Tehran has demonstrated how less powerful countries can stymie more powerful ones in the modern battlefield. More powerful countries will also embrace offensive strategies that depend on precise mass, since the cost of defending against cheap munitions remains much greater than the cost of attacking with them.
As the world learns this lesson, the United States must as well. The country’s reliance on exquisite, expensive, hard-to-produce weapons is no longer enough to win wars and protect allies, especially given that the United States is drawing down missile stockpiles needed to deter China and others. Ideally, Washington would start scaling precise mass, investing heavily in low-cost defenses, and, crucially, adapting its organizational structures to use these tools effectively. American defense officials—accustomed to fighting only with exquisite systems—may struggle to accept this needed shift, especially if the defense budget shrinks, which could easily lead Washington to prioritize older and proven legacy capabilities, no matter their limits. And even if the Pentagon starts making changes, the country will require talented military commanders and senior civilian defense officials to stay in power long enough to drive these innovations through. Right now, the Pentagon is rapidly churning through both types of leaders.
Americans should hope that Washington will find a way forward. New innovations have, at least for now, closed the military gap between rich states and poor ones when it comes to offensive capacities. If the United States wants to maintain its military edge, it has no choice but to embrace precise mass—and stop carrying on as if the Cold War just ended.
articles.summary: The lessons of Tehran’s use of precise mass.

articles.title: The Coming Taiwan Crisis
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
JONATHAN A. CZIN is Michael H. Armacost Chair in Foreign Policy Studies at the Brookings Institution’s China Center and a co-host of the podcast The Beijing Brief. He was Director for China at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2023 and previously served as a member of the Senior Analytic Service at the Central Intelligence Agency. The views expressed here are his own.
As U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet in Washington this week, the Taiwan Strait, the waterway that has long been a flashpoint between the two countries, has seemed remarkably quiet. Chinese fighter jets regularly cross the centerline between Taiwan and the mainland. Chinese warships maneuver to the east of the island. And Beijing uses its coast guard to continually harass ships in the area. Yet for nearly a year, Beijing has avoided the large-scale military exercises that had become a regular feature of its coercion of Taiwan after former U.S. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s visit to the island, in 2022.
That shift stems in large part from renewed optimism in Beijing. Although the Trump administration has not formally changed its policy toward Taiwan, Trump’s statements after his prior meeting with Xi in May undermined Taipei’s confidence in the United States’ commitment to the island. “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent,” he said at the time. “And, you know, we’re supposed to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war. I'm not looking for that.”
For years, many in Washington and across the Asia-Pacific region assumed that 2027 would be the next potential pivot point for Beijing’s Taiwan policy, because Xi had directed the People’s Liberation Army to be prepared for a cross-strait military confrontation by that date. Yet as 2027 approaches, it appears exceedingly unlikely that Xi is gearing up to employ lethal force any time soon. Xi has been willing to conduct systematic purges of his military high command, in part because he is not worried about a cross-strait crisis in the near future. For now, Xi seems to feel confident that he can effectively manage both Washington and Taipei.
But Xi remains deadly serious about organizing his force for a conflict over Taiwan in the coming years. The next pivotal date will not be 2027, when Xi is expected to begin a fourth term, but 2028, when both the United States and Taiwan will hold presidential elections that will determine the future trajectory of the cross-strait dynamic. In all likelihood, Xi will find himself frustrated by the outcome of Taiwan’s next election, which will make the situation more fraught than it is now. The coming two years are thus a crucial window for Washington to work with Taipei to prepare for what will likely be a far more turbulent period in the Taiwan Strait after 2028.
Rather than let doubts about its support for Taipei deepen, Washington should lean into its relationship with the island. In many ways, Taiwan has refashioned itself into a model partner, both by reorienting its economy toward the United States and away from China and by boosting investments in its own defense. At the very least, Trump should approve the $14 billion arms package that is on his desk, even if that means dividing the sale into smaller tranches to avoid escalating tensions with Beijing.
China will not welcome a series of U.S. arms sales, but historically Beijing has shown far more concern for high-profile gestures of political support for Taiwan, such as Pelosi’s visit, than over the bureaucratic details of U.S. weapons transfers. And leaving arms sales in abeyance carries its own long-term costs. By forgoing this minimum step, the administration will be complicit in Beijing’s bid to establish a veto over U.S. arms sales and, by extension, over the cross-strait dynamic. After 2028, the diplomatic price of such support for Taipei is likely to rise, as an aging Xi may conclude that further delay on Taiwan no longer works in his favor.
Xi’s optimism is predicated on the hope that the opposition Kuomintang party (KMT) will regain power in 2028 after a dozen years of rule by the Democratic Progressive Party, which the mainland reviles as separatist. Beijing has had no visible engagement with the government since the DPP came to power in 2016—a marked departure from Xi’s approach to the previous administration. In 2015, Xi became the first Chinese leader since Mao Zedong to shake hands with his Taiwanese counterpart, a precedent he must have relished. Yet rather than becoming part and parcel of what Xi and his propagandists call the “new era” for China under his rule, Taiwan has steadily drifted away from the mainland, frustrating his ambitions to begin the political process of annexing the island. Annexation, not a costly and likely catastrophic military invasion, is his ultimate goal.
Xi’s hopes rose in November 2025, when Cheng Li-wun unexpectedly became chair of the KMT. Cheng has advocated a much softer line toward China, emphasizing the common Chineseness of citizens on both sides of the strait and the need for cross-strait dialogue. In April 2026, she traveled to Beijing to meet with Xi just weeks before he hosted Trump. The meeting positioned Xi to depict his Taiwan policy as conciliatory and reasonable, despite his hard-line approach to the ruling party over the past decade. His willingness to receive Cheng signals that she has become the linchpin of his hopes for advancing discussions about Taiwan’s status after 2028. Yet hope is not a strategy, and Cheng’s prospects even for becoming the KMT’s candidate in 2028, let alone for prevailing in the general election, are precarious. Her pro-Beijing views are not widely shared even within her own party. Cheng was a dark-horse candidate who secured the position of the KMT chair with just over 50 percent of the votes, and only 27 percent of the population supports her party.
That means that in 2028, Xi will likely confront either a fourth consecutive DPP administration under current President Lai Ching-te or a more moderate KMT leader who is warier than Cheng of Xi’s embrace. Should Lai secure a second term along with a renewed majority in Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan, it would devastate Xi’s hope that the KMT offers a viable alternative. After Lai’s victory in the 2024 election, Beijing consoled itself with the fact that he prevailed with just a plurality of the vote and lost control of the legislature to the KMT; it spun the result as a sign that most of Taiwan’s voters did not support Lai’s approach to the mainland. That was not just propaganda but a genuine rationalization for the manifest failure of Beijing’s cross-strait policies. Those shortcomings will be harder to explain away in 2028, especially if voters treat another Lai victory as a rebuke of the KMT’s more conciliatory posture. Xi at that point would be the steward of a stagnant Taiwan policy that has produced no political progress over more than a dozen years.
Xi’s looming dilemma underscores the hollowness of the Chinese Communist Party’s Taiwan strategy. His predecessor, Hu Jintao, tried a softer approach toward the KMT administration of Ma Ying-jeou, but the effort backfired. In 2014, young protesters in the Sunflower Movement occupied Taiwan’s legislature amid widespread opposition to a trade deal meant to deepen cross-strait integration. When the DPP took power in 2016, Xi—who had already demonstrated his comfort with a more muscular national security policy—shifted to coercion without diplomacy, cutting off all visible channels of communication with Taiwan’s political leadership. The goal has been to convince the people of Taiwan that the status quo is unsustainable, that annexation is inevitable, and that they should therefore acquiesce to Beijing’s overtures.
Xi is likely to be more impatient about resolving the Taiwan issue in his fourth term; by the end of it, he will be nearly 80. Although he may now feel that time is on his side, he is less likely to feel that way then. And especially if he is frustrated by Taiwan’s 2028 election outcome, he may be tempted to reach for more coercive actions. Xi likely learned from the Pelosi kerfuffle that he can go quite far in threatening the island: China’s over-the-top response in 2022 included firing PLA missiles over Taiwan for the first time since the Taiwan Strait crisis of the 1990s, as well as imposing maritime exclusion zones around the island. Yet it did not provoke a full-blown crisis with the United States or cause tangible repercussions for China. Xi also may have more confidence in his high command after the CCP’s 21st Congress, next year, when he will reshuffle his leadership team. He will presumably finish replacing the dozens of senior officers he has purged during his third term and may reorganize the military’s top ranks altogether.
But Xi would have to go beyond his 2022 response to make Taipei and Washington heed his grievances. This might include a more sustained, punitive, and risky military pressure campaign, even if no shots were fired, such as stopping foreign ships at sea, declaring multiple zones near Taiwan off-limits to international maritime traffic, and seeking to disrupt high-profile U.S. arms deliveries on commercial carriers. That would fall short of the full-blown blockade or quarantine that many in Washington have long feared, but it would send the message that Taiwan remains connected to the outside world only with Beijing’s acquiescence.
Yet in any such scenario, the off-ramp and the endgame are unclear. A Chinese decision to escalate might push Taiwan’s voters toward grudging acceptance of rule by the mainland—but it might just as easily backfire, creating a rally-around-the-flag effect on the island and augmenting anti-Beijing sentiment. That is what happened in the wake of the third Taiwan Strait crisis, in the 1990s, when Beijing’s threats against the DPP before the 2000 election helped the party win its first presidential race.
Xi could, of course, go for a full blockade or quarantine, or even seize one of the islands that Taiwan governs that sit alarmingly close to the mainland. Yet over 14 years in office he has shown that he is neither impulsive nor especially violent in his conduct of foreign policy, preferring steady, incremental pressure over a single decisive blow. Those riskier options could very well fail, undermining the premise that has animated him for decades: to secure his legacy as the leader who set Taiwan on the path toward what Beijing calls “reunification.” A quarantine or blockade would also play in some ways to the strengths of the United States in a crisis, allowing it time to muster a coalition of the willing to impose costs on Beijing.
These more violent options could become more tempting for Xi if a so-called restrainer who is suspicious of traditional U.S. partnerships enters the White House after the 2028 U.S. election. Such a president might be skeptical of U.S. interests in Taiwan, or of reinvigorating the alliances and partnerships that the United States would need to marshal to protect it. Even if a more conventional candidate prevails in 2028, China will likely have learned a great deal from the current war in Iran about the limits of U.S. power and Washington’s political and material ability to persevere. Key U.S. munitions stocks will take years to rebuild, and the conflict with Iran has exposed the vulnerability of U.S. overseas bases and naval logistics. Those problems will persist into the next administration, constraining the ability of the United States to respond to China in a crisis, regardless of what U.S. policymakers might want to do.
In the meantime, the United States and Taiwan have an opportunity to toughen up the island while Xi waits to see what the 2028 elections bring. Under the DPP, Taiwan has ended years of complacency about the threat from the mainland. It has stepped up investment in its own defense and pivoted its economy away from China more than almost any other country, including the United States. It has also demonstrated the will, the wherewithal, and now an incipient capacity to confront the challenge before it.
Most notably, after years of procuring U.S. weapons systems that would be useless in a conflict with China, Taiwan has finally gotten serious about defense reform. In May, it passed a supplemental bill appropriating $25 billion for the military. One of the central challenges facing that military now is not just how to acquire new capabilities but how to integrate them into the force. Indeed, the most contested political issue on Taiwan this year was defense reform, particularly appropriations for expanding the domestic drone industry. The KMT held up the legislation before acquiescing ahead of the island’s midterm elections, which will take place in November. Yet the mere fact that this is what the parties are fighting over is itself a hopeful sign of the government’s concern about defense.
The program for toughening Taiwan is not limited to the military. The government is serious about the trickier task of enhancing “whole-of-society resilience,” a delicate balancing act of acclimating the public to the threat from the mainland—and the possibility that it might one day invade or blockade the island—without inducing panic or resignation. Taiwan’s private sector shares many of the same temptations as firms around the world to buy cheaper Chinese goods, but the government is intent on keeping “red” components out of supply chains for government procurement.
Meanwhile, Taiwan’s economy is growing at a breathtaking rate, which means that it will have the fiscal space to fund military modernization in the coming years. It also has become far less dependent on China economically. Whereas in 2010 more than 80 percent of Taiwan’s outbound investment went to China, today less than ten percent does. Taiwan’s growth is instead fueled by its world-class semiconductor industry, which has capitalized on the AI boom. With a population of only 23 million, Taiwan has catapulted to become the fourth-largest trading partner of the United States. And it is not just selling its wares there: its leading companies have promised to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in the U.S. economy. In February, Taiwan became one of the first countries to finalize a trade deal with the Trump administration. Unlike most U.S. trade partners, Taiwan seems genuinely pleased with the outcome, because it narrows the gap between the tariff rate on Taiwan’s goods and the rates on goods from its regional competitors Japan and South Korea.
Unfortunately, rather than capitalizing on these deepening economic ties and on Taipei’s serious approach to defense, Washington is undermining them. The structural forces all favor a closer relationship, but the diplomacy—which should be the easiest part of getting this right—has become the weakest pillar. Trump’s May visit to Beijing stoked anxiety in Taipei that he would sell out the island’s interests with a grand gesture. Instead, the president was at pains to stay on message for most of the trip, only to fumble in the comfortable setting of a Fox News interview. Trump described arms sales as a bargaining chip he could use with Beijing, unsettling decades of precedent whereby American presidents refused to consult Chinese leaders on the subject. In the days and weeks afterward, top U.S. officials emphasized that policy toward Taiwan had not changed, but the damage had been done.
More seasoned observers of U.S. policy on Taiwan were rattled less by the president’s rhetoric than by his actions, particularly his hesitation in moving forward on the $14 billion arms package. As a practical matter, the deficiencies of the U.S. defense industrial base and procurement process mean that the capabilities in that package would not arrive in Taiwan before the end of Trump’s term, which explains his lack of enthusiasm for it. And even once the materiel arrives, Taiwan will need time to assimilate its capabilities into its force so that it can employ them effectively.
But the long lead times only underscore the need for the administration to make haste now, when it has a willing partner in Taiwan with the fiscal space to make these purchases, and when Xi is waiting to see what 2028 will bring. The next administration may not have such a good opportunity to enhance Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities, and Taiwan will need all the capacity it can muster to deal with an aging and potentially more cantankerous Xi.
If the KMT wins in 2028, it may also lack the DPP’s enthusiasm for defense cooperation with Washington. Meanwhile, Xi is in the midst of a painful renovation of his military high command, which, when finished, could change the calculus in its own way. Thus, the fragile gentleman’s agreement between Trump and Xi could afford the diplomatic space to take advantage of this window without precipitating a crisis.

articles.title: The Price of Arctic Ambition
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
IRIS FERGUSON is a Visiting Scholar at Penn Washington. From 2022 to 2025, she served as U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Arctic and Global Resilience.
In 2016, a crack in the ice opened beneath the site of the U.S. Navy’s flagship Arctic exercise several hundred miles north of Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, forcing experiments to end early and leaving researchers scrambling to evacuate. Five years later, an early freeze trapped roughly two dozen commercial vessels in the East Siberian Sea; some had to wait weeks for Russian icebreaker assistance. And during a Canadian-led multinational military exercise in 2025, allied forces encountered a difficult combination of conditions: extreme cold grounded helicopters, broke snowmobiles, and knocked out communications equipment even as thinning sea ice forced U.S. pilots to search 25,000 miles of coastline for a location thick enough to land on.
These were not failures by unprepared or inexperienced Arctic actors. They involved three of the region’s most proficient nations, each operating in territory it knew well. But there was a common thread: the Arctic has a way of humbling those who operate there. Its distances, darkness, extreme weather, and sparse infrastructure expose the limits of even the most capable governments and militaries.
This fact creates a paradox. The Arctic is a main approach to the U.S. homeland and a platform for projecting power at the top of the world. That is precisely why, as geopolitical competition intensifies, Washington is becoming increasingly focused on protecting sovereignty and securing its interests in the region. Yet no single country, not even the United States, can see, maneuver, and sustain itself across the Arctic. Effective sovereignty there relies on building networks of dependence.
This week’s agreement between Greenland, Denmark, and the United States illustrates the point. After months of negotiation, the three parties struck a symbiotic deal codifying U.S. military access while affirming Danish and Greenlandic self-governance. U.S. President Donald Trump has called it a win for American interests; Denmark and Greenland a win for sovereignty. Both are true, as nearly every mission that makes Greenland strategically valuable—missile warning, submarine detection, basing, and resupply—works because the United States is embedded in an alliance system.
The agreement could mark a turning point in how Washington approaches Arctic security. Trump’s early talk of acquiring Greenland or making Canada the 51st U.S. state cast self-reliance as the goal and strained relations with key Arctic partners. This agreement signals a more productive direction. Working with allies preserves the advantages the United States already holds and closes the gaps, in both presence and allied political unity, that adversaries are eager to exploit.
But fully embracing the role that allies and partners must play for the United States to achieve its goals in the Arctic will require a shift in a long-held mindset. For the United States, pursuing interdependence is an uncomfortable strategy. Self-reliance remains closely associated with national power, and Washington has historically approached Arctic shortfalls by asking what additional U.S. capabilities it needs to generate. Decades of deprioritizing the Arctic, however, coupled with the region’s vast and forbidding geography, leave the United States with little choice but to work closely with partners. In practice, the interdependence it needs to have with allies in the Arctic is already found everywhere—now Washington must continue to build on it.
The United States’ basic ability to understand and communicate what is happening in the vast Arctic region depends on partnerships. Arctic awareness remains uniquely fragmented across three distinct regions: North America, Europe, and the Pacific. Information is further dispersed across a variety of militaries, scientific institutions, intelligence agencies, and local indigenous communities, whose knowledge of the changing environment far exceeds any new sensor.
Since the early 1960s, just after the creation of the U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), the United States has intentionally based some of its most important missile-defense systems in Canada and Greenland. Because of gaps in its own coverage, the United States now relies on a Japanese satellite to detect the extent of Arctic sea ice, which is integral to understanding the evolution of commercial and military sea routes. The United States further depends on allied monitoring over the European Arctic to understand threats approaching U.S. territory and on allied judgment to interpret competitors’ intent in the Arctic. Nordic nations have decades of experience observing the Russian military’s behavior around the Kola Peninsula, home to much of the country’s nuclear capacity, making their observations indispensable to Washington’s ability to distinguish between routine and escalatory behavior. The United States, for its part, can see patterns of Chinese and Russian activity near Alaska that European allies might miss.
The United States already gains a great deal of visibility from its allies in the Arctic, but the systems are not always designed to connect across geographies and stakeholders. NORAD and NATO, for instance, each hold a piece of the Arctic picture, yet information and communications do not flow seamlessly between them. Addressing this problem does not require one overarching operational picture or surrendering control of sensitive information; it requires the United States to play the same standard-setting role it has long played to keep allied systems interoperable. That matters even more now as allies build sovereign sensors and communications networks on their own. Scientific cooperation deserves a similarly intentional and collaborative approach. Because the Arctic changes faster than anywhere else on Earth, climate and environmental research is increasingly integral to understanding operating conditions from submarine sonar to search and rescue, as well as wildfire risk.
The United States’ reliance on partners in the Arctic becomes even more obvious when Washington needs to move. It faces a distinctive geographic dilemma: it seeks to project power into both the Atlantic and Pacific sides of the region, but Alaska is its sole sovereign Arctic territory. Everywhere else across the North Atlantic and European Arctic, the United States’ reach runs through allies.
The United States has spent decades building that access. In 2018, when the USS Harry S. Truman conducted the first U.S. carrier strike group operation in the Arctic since the Cold War, it depended on Norwegian and NATO logistics and resupply and on the shelter of Norway’s fjords when a storm swelled seas to 30 feet. In 2023, Iceland allowed a U.S. nuclear-powered submarine to sail into its territorial waters to receive supplies and exchange crew for the first time. The following year, Finland, Norway, and Sweden signed defense cooperation agreements granting the United States access to dozens of sites. These agreements were not favors. They reflected Nordic states’ calculation that U.S. presence, equipment, and resupply strengthen deterrence against Russia and a recognition that allied geography and U.S. military capacity are most valuable when joined.
The United States does not need to be everywhere in the Arctic; indeed, it cannot be. Even as the Pentagon deepens operational ties with allied Arctic militaries, Washington should empower its allies to take primary responsibility where they are best positioned to act—which would constitute a meaningful form of burden sharing within NATO. For example, Norway and other Nordic states have been leading efforts to invest in infrastructure, platforms, and sensors to monitor Russian hybrid activity such as undersea cable sabotage and GPS jamming along the northern approaches to the Atlantic. Sharing this burden would allow the United States to concentrate more attention and resources on Alaska and the Pacific Arctic, where decades of underinvestment affect nearly every category of Arctic infrastructure—ports, icebreakers, runways, energy systems, and search and rescue.
Beyond the need to think creatively about access, the Arctic offers an increasing number of opportunities to advance allied industrial capacity, even in areas such as space programs and icebreakers, which Washington has long treated as symbols of national power. Many Arctic systems are unusually specialized and expensive, requiring industrial capacity and expertise that few countries can sustain on their own. Icebreakers are a case in point. After years spent struggling to rebuild its own fleet, in 2024 the United States turned to Canada and Finland to cooperate on pooling shipyards, knowledge, and labor. Over time, this effort will not only create much-needed additional maritime presence but will also help rebuild U.S. expertise and the broader allied shipbuilding base.
Washington should embrace that model rather than treat it as an exception. It could lead the development of an Arctic industrial strategy that draws on the best capabilities across the alliance. Doing so would allow the United States to leverage its own defense industrial base while continuing to shape the standards and interoperability that make allied systems work.
There are obvious opportunities for such a strategy. Washington could facilitate collaborative architectures for Arctic military satellite communications that ensure nations can interact smoothly during a crisis. It could invite select allies—Canada, at a minimum—to participate in the ground- or space-based elements of the Golden Dome missile defense system, extending the coverage and redundancy that allied geography already provides. It could coordinate with allies on producing cold-weather gear unique to the North American Arctic climate, allowing for cost sharing. It could pool research for energy technologies such as cold-hardened batteries and small modular reactors that would aid troops’ operational reach and give off-grid communities alternatives to costly diesel generators. And it could pursue critical mineral development and processing deals, including stockpiling, to shore up supply chains that underpin many new technologies.
Such a collaborative industrial strategy would not require the United States to become overly dependent on single suppliers, nor would it demand the creation of sprawling multinational procurement programs. Instead, the United States and its allies would make deliberate choices about what each would build, what they would buy from one another, and where developing capabilities together would make more sense than duplicating scarce expertise.
The United States’ top rivals already understand the value of Arctic cooperation. Although Russia controls roughly half of the Arctic coastline, it is increasingly turning toward China for capital, infrastructure development, satellite-based positioning and navigation, and scientific endeavors in the region. The two countries have no guarantee that their long-term interests will align, but they are deepening their interdependence in the Arctic nonetheless.
The United States begins from a far more advantageous position. It possesses allies across the Arctic and beyond whose geography, expertise, infrastructure, and industrial capabilities complement its own, and if organized intentionally, those alliances will become an indisputable source of strength.
Operational cooperation among Arctic allies is arguably at an all-time high. Nordic integration, expanded NATO planning, and new industrial partnerships have created unprecedented opportunities for collective action. But the United States’ ability to take advantage of them depends on sustaining trust, both with allied capitals and with indigenous communities whose knowledge and voices are integral to decisions about the region’s future.
Washington has tested this trust. The recent negotiated deal is a real step toward restoring it, but some allies are already hedging. In 2025, when the United States briefly suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, several Arctic allies moved to invest in their own satellite and surveillance capabilities to reduce their dependence on Washington. Others have sought to diminish their reliance on U.S. defense technologies. And after Washington’s early rhetoric on Greenland, even closely aligned capitals have privately wondered whether U.S. access could become a source of leverage rather than reassurance.
This is why political cohesion should be treated as a pillar of operational capability. The instinct to maximize the United States’ control and freedom of action can have the opposite effect if it weakens the relationships on which U.S. action depends. The United States does not become more powerful in the Arctic by making allies less willing to share information, provide access, or build alongside it.
Critics of interdependence may say that relying on other countries creates its own vulnerability. A partner can fail to share intelligence quickly enough, deny access, or lack capacity when it is most needed. But self-sufficiency carries its own risks, particularly when it exists more in political rhetoric than operational reality. A United States that talks like a leading Arctic power without the capabilities to match is weaker than one that relies deliberately on trusted allies.
Since the United States unveiled its first Arctic Strategy in 1994, it has espoused grand visions for the region, promising to protect both its interests and the environment. But multiple administrations over the course of three decades have never fully resourced these plans. This is not a failure, since the Arctic has never been Washington’s only priority, but it is a pattern Washington can no longer afford to follow as the region changes and competitors move to fill the gaps. A realist’s reading of history leads to one conclusion: Washington’s ambitions can be achieved only by relying on partners. In the Arctic, the cold reality is that the future will be shaped by the coalition best able to act in concert, not by the country that tries to guard its sovereignty alone.
articles.summary: The Greenland deal proves self-reliance is not an option.

articles.title: How Putin Escalates
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ANDREI KOLESNIKOV is the author of The Closing of the Russian Mind: How Putin's Ideology Took the Nation Hostage.
The overwhelming victory of President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party in last weekend’s parliamentary elections was not only expected but planned. Compulsory voting in organizations dependent on the budget and in many corporations; standardized voting in the military, law enforcement agencies, and the so-called new territories; mechanical voting in the spirit of “take my vote and leave me alone”; the spread of electronic voting; and the pre-election removal of Yabloko, the only antiwar party still operating legally—all these and other factors assured a supermajority for the ruling party. Even votes cast for other parliamentary parties amounted to support for the government, because they, too, are controlled by the Kremlin.
Nonetheless, for Putin, this refreshed mandate offers renewed legitimacy for his “special military operation” in Ukraine, showing domestically what the Kremlin is projecting internationally: that Russia is in a position of strength and is ready to pursue its military objectives with even more abandon. The Kremlin’s main goal is to create the illusion of a total commanding majority, regardless of the actual situation. Everyone supports Putin, the results convey, and therefore they must also support the country’s military policies, relentless suppression of dissent, and anti-Western course; those who oppose him are outcasts and pariahs. Indeed, since 2022, elections in Russia have redefined citizenship as support for the war.
Reality is more complicated. Since April, public polling in Russia has consistently signaled that things are not going very well for the government. According to the independent Levada Center, which has been regularly asking the question, in July, the percentage of respondents who considered the special operation a success had fallen to 50 percent, a drop of nearly 20 percentage points from the previous year. In the same poll, the number of people who believed the country was moving in the right direction had fallen by ten percentage points from a year earlier, to 54 percent. Moreover, between July 2025 and July 2026, the president’s own approval rating declined 12 percent—a very significant drop in a personalist autocracy.
Alongside this, general public morale has steadily declined. There is now constant anxiety over the protracted war and the possibility of further military mobilization, as well as about inflation, far-reaching Internet restrictions, and an unending fuel crisis. According to Levada Center surveys done in August, two-thirds of respondents said they faced problems with mobile Internet access, messaging apps, and gasoline shortages. Gasoline shortages seriously disrupted the lives of one in three respondents, while Internet restrictions affected one in five. Massive military spending and rising fuel prices have been major drivers of inflation, and starting in October, a spike in utility rates will add to those pressures.
Now that elections have taken place, many Russians fear another military mobilization, although the Kremlin—wary of undermining the illusion of a somewhat normal life amid a war that has reached the heart of Russia in the form of drone attacks—seems to prefer selective and covert mobilization over a general call-up. But other new pressures cannot be ruled out. As long as Putin believes that time is on his side, and the people—apparently hypnotized by what the Kremlin calls the “unity” demonstrated during the elections—are ready to bear the burden of troubles, he will continue the war. And continuing means escalating, abroad and at home.
Already, the Russian president has rejected a new U.S. diplomatic push and stepped up the pace and nature of attacks in Ukraine. Meanwhile, pro-Kremlin foreign policy experts speak of the various ways, both nonnuclear and nuclear, that Russia can escalate further, especially during the coming winter, when the Kremlin plans to literally freeze Ukraine by striking its power grid. For Putin, escalation has become a principal means for maintaining power.
For weeks now, there have been many indications that Putin is preparing for a new stage in Russia’s conflict with Ukraine and the West. The Kremlin has been stoking a continual sense of emergency, peddling threats—what the late Russian political scientist Gleb Pavlovsky called the “Russian conflict conveyor belt,” a machine that must never be allowed to stop. At the same time, the government has imposed a siege mentality on the public, along with the need to maintain absolute unity, a dynamic that has been reinforced by the intensification of Ukrainian airstrikes deep inside Russia. This kind of threat amplification explains the sweeping crackdown on Yabloko in the runup to the parliamentary elections. Not only was the party banned from taking part in the elections, its members were arrested and one of its leaders, Lev Shlosberg, was sentenced to 11 years in prison. When a country requires a unified national mindset, no anti-war voice can be legally heard.
Meanwhile, Putin has been taking trips, hosting meetings, and delivering speeches with abnormal frequency. He has addressed the military, children, scientists, and businesspeople, and even visited a disputed island in the Sea of Okhotsk with the clear aim of angering and provoking Japan. (The island is known as Iturup in Russia and Etorofu in Japan.) At the same time, since the summer, the Kremlin has stepped up its efforts to keep the masses emotionally and spiritually mobilized around the “special military operation.” No part of Russian culture, society, or history is overlooked.
In August, for example, the Russian Orthodox Church announced that the remains of Dmitry Donskoy—the legendary fourteenth-century warrior-prince who defeated the Tatars of the Mongol Horde at the Battle of Kulikovo—had been unexpectedly “discovered” at the Cathedral of the Archangel in Moscow. Immediately, Putin visited the place of burial and this historic prince was conscripted into military service—part of his relics were sent to the front to “spiritually strengthen” the Russian units fighting there. When a war drags on for so long, Russians can pin their hopes not only on the “miracle weapons” Putin boasts about but also simply on a miracle. Even as the parliamentary elections took place, thousands of Orthodox Christians were lining up to view the relics of Saint Spyridon of Trimythous in Moscow, as though they had come to vote for him. Across the country, hundreds of thousands of believers have also taken part in government-supported religious processions that are aimed at bolstering support for the armed forces. The most impressive of these was the huge, ultra-nationalist “Russian March” that took place in Moscow in early September.
The only question is: what constitutes a miracle? For most Russians, it is the end of the war. Sooner or later, Putin will have to extricate himself from the conflict, and no one but the United States can help him do that. The Trump administration appears to be making a new attempt at negotiations, ideally with a different strategy than the Anchorage summit or the Witkoff-Kushner-style “tourist diplomacy” that characterized the administration’s first year. But no replacement for this model has yet been found. CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s August blitz visit to Moscow seemed to be part of an effort to pursue a new type of diplomacy, perhaps something more like the back channel that was established between U.S. National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger and the Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin during the era of détente. So far, it is hard to envision how a genuine, permanent channel might emerge that could steer both sides toward peace and, among other things, ease tensions between Russia and the United States. Still, for U.S. President Donald Trump, there are also new reasons to push this. After a string of spectacular foreign policy failures and facing a tough midterm election of his own, Trump urgently needs a success story.
For now, the Kremlin believes that it has both time and the means to continue fighting for as long as it takes. Putin is incapable of doubting that he is right. Along with the stage-managed Duma elections, the purging of any trace of antiwar rhetoric from the public sphere is intended to grant Putin a stronger mandate for whatever actions he sees fit to take. An unknown question is how far into the future Russians are prepared to grant this legitimacy.
So far, it has been up to citizens themselves to cope with the burning oil refineries, destroyed warehouses, empty gas stations, nonfunctioning Internet, and life-threatening risks from drone attacks. In addition to chronic inflation, the budget deficit has become a problem, and Russia’s GDP and industrial production are hovering just above zero. This is despite the fact that, until recently, arms production had formally kept these indicators at a moderately high level; now, even that is no longer helping.
In the face of these challenges, people are bearing with the system for now. It is also worth noting that the same surveys that show Russians are less satisfied with the special military operation than they were before also show that greater numbers of them prefer intensifying strikes over making concessions to achieve peace. More than half of the respondents in an August Levada Center poll think it is likely that the special military operation will last another year, and the number of those who say they are certain of this has grown. Precisely because of their utter exhaustion with war, many see increased military activity as a way to bring peace closer.
But if the Kremlin demands another rally around the flag—especially one that involves mobilizing large segments of the male population—it might tip the situation against Putin. Rumors about such a move, which could also be part of a broader Russian escalation, have been circulating for weeks, even though the changed nature of the war has made sending more men to the battlefield a pointless waste, and also risks diverting the remaining labor force away from doing needed jobs at home, not to mention the damage to the demographic situation, including the decreasing birth-rate. Still, it cannot be ruled out.
Putin still portrays what Russia is doing as a historically just defensive campaign of liberation. This is not unlike how Stalin portrayed the 1939 Winter War with Finland, or the Red Army’s “liberation campaign” in that same year, which led to the incorporation of western Belarus and western Ukraine into the Soviet Union. But to be a “people’s war,” as Kremlin propagandists and officials have sometimes referred to the special operation, the conflict must have a limited time frame. It also must, in principle, end in victory for the people, whatever that may mean. (Under current circumstances, Russians will accept any version of victory, as long as they are told that the goals have been achieved on Russia’s terms—that is how exhausted people have become.)
In reality, the “special military operation” has taken on the characteristics of a personal war waged by the head of state. In fact, from the very beginning, it was a personal war that simply involved the people in a wide variety of ways, including physical participation in combat operations and forced submission to political rules, restrictions, and systematic repression. For decades, Russians have been conditioned to live in a state of preparation for war, or, more precisely, for wars. Such a constant war footing—and actual war and the relentless militarization of economy—is what ultimately caused the Soviet system to buckle. Putin has revived this approach to serve his own goal of reconstituting Russia’s empire, but Russians may not be prepared to have their society so strongly militarized, knowing that they, too, might be mobilized or have drones hit their roofs, indefinitely. It is possible to adapt to such a world and it is possible to normalize it. But for how long?
In Putin’s Russia, escalation happens on two different fronts. It is taking place on the battlefield, but it is taking place at home as well. The signs are almost everywhere. There is the continual arrest and imprisonment of those who disagree with the Kremlin’s policies, a practice that has become increasingly brutal. There is the persistent tightening, to the point of absurdity, of legislation regarding “foreign agents,” especially those who have left the country, who are now deprived not only of political rights but also of property and financial rights. There is the increasingly unsustainable tax burden, because the regime lacks the funds for war. (The Kremlin raised Russia’s value-added tax this year from 20 to 22 percent, a levy that weighs especially heavily on small and medium-sized businesses.)
In international analysis of Russian strategy, the home front is often forgotten, but it is just as important. One form of escalation cannot exist without the other. Without increasing internal pressure, the regime cannot ratchet up its external actions. Manufacturing crises has become the basis of Putin’s system and the mechanism by which he maintains his power. Yet the returns on this strategy—which he masterfully sustained by misleading Trump in 2025 and derailing the prospect of peace talks in the first half of 2026—are diminishing. Even the regime’s own spin now bears the hallmarks of hysteria. Officials such as Pyotr Tolstoy, deputy speaker of parliament and former TV host, openly speak of the need to strike at the enemy’s civilian population in order to demoralize it. Hate speech and the glorification of cruelty and violence have become another form of escalation. But again, the effect wears off with frequent use.
The Kremlin’s current embrace of escalation of every kind is not a sign of strength but of weakness. The elections have allowed Putin to bind Russians to his “special military operation” through the voting process: anyone who participated in elections has become an accomplice. But this will likely only exacerbate the frustration of many people who are tired of the living conditions imposed by the state. No one will protest; many will feign support. But just as in the late Soviet years, the very act of existing within such a system will look like the imitation of normalcy rather than the real thing. There is no longer a clear way out for a country traumatized by war, befuddled by the propaganda of violence and the ideology of national superiority, and damaged by a distorted and increasingly dysfunctional war economy.
The Putin regime’s greatest crisis is a crisis of the future. It doesn’t know where to go or why. And so it prolongs the war as a means of survival. The U.S. administration is trying to show Putin an off-ramp by dangling huge business deals or, if that status quo continues, threatening to impose “hellish” sanctions. But the most realistic scenario right now is that Putin will continue to stall for time, using winter as a weapon.
articles.summary: A new stage in Russia's confrontation with Ukraine—and the West.

articles.title: The Stalemate With Iran Is Not Sustainable
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
RICHARD HAASS is President Emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, Senior Counselor at Centerview Partners, and the author of the Substack newsletter Home & Away.
CAROLYN KISSANE is Associate Dean and Clinical Professor at the New York University School of Professional Studies Center for Global Affairs, Founding Director of NYU’s Global Energy, Climate, and Sustainability Lab, and the author of the Substack newsletter Energy Common Sense.
For six months, the war with Iran was disruptive but manageable. The Strait of Hormuz was largely closed to maritime traffic, blocking a transit route for roughly 20 percent of the world’s liquefied natural gas trade and an even higher proportion of the oil trade. Prices ticked upward and many parts of the world struggled with oil and gas shortages, but countries found ways to help stabilize the global energy market. The United States and Iran both refrained from overly destructive attacks on the Gulf region’s vital energy infrastructure. It seemed that Washington and Tehran could extend their current stalemate, occasionally trading airstrikes and attacks on individual tankers and energy facilities, without leading the world into economic calamity.
That is no longer the case. The war has now expanded to critical parts of the region’s energy infrastructure, including the very routes that had been making it possible to offset the asphyxiation of the Strait of Hormuz. As of mid-September, the Bab el Mandeb Strait—a maritime chokepoint along the Red Sea route that is the main alternative to shipping oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz—is under the control of the Houthis, a Yemeni-based group aligned with Iran. And a drone launched by an Iranian-affiliated militia operating out of Iraq struck the East–West pipeline in Saudi Arabia, through which the kingdom had diverted a large portion of its oil exports. The attack temporarily disabled the pipeline.
As a result, the price of oil jumped from the mid $70s in August to $110 per barrel in September. And if the rest of the region’s energy infrastructure is no longer off limits to military attack, further supply interruptions could easily push oil prices to $150 or even $200 a barrel. An escalation of fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, which has become a very real risk since the Houthis launched attacks on the Saudi cities of Riyadh and Yanbu last week, would add to the upward pressure on prices. If that happens, an energy crisis that plunges the world into recession is not far off.
Washington must now find a way out of this untenable situation. Half a year of alternating military attacks and economic coercion has not forced Tehran and its partners to make concessions, and there is no reason to expect that those strategies—much less threatening to “annihilate” Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump did in his UN speech on Tuesday—would compel them to change their behavior today. Nor would it be possible for the United States and its allies to protect energy infrastructure and shipments indefinitely under threat of attack by Iran and other hostile actors.
The least bad option is a return to diplomacy. The United States needs to try to reach an agreement with Iran to end the war, one that includes not just a cease-fire but also a plan for keeping vital waterways open and measures that induce Tehran to comply with its terms. Washington must also encourage Saudi Arabia to pursue a similar settlement with the Houthis. Brokering these truces will require painful concessions from both Washington and Riyadh. But continuing to fight this war would court economic disaster, and that would be far more painful.
At the start of the war, many economists and analysts feared that the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz would provoke an acute energy crisis and economic downturn, or worse. Their concerns were reasonable. Before the conflict began, nearly 20 million barrels of crude oil and refined products passed through the strait each day, along with close to one-fifth of globally traded liquefied natural gas. By August, energy exports were running at roughly half their prewar level. Some days, fewer than ten ships traversed the strait—far fewer than in peacetime, when between 130 and 150 commercial vessels would make the passage each day.
Yet the global energy system proved remarkably capable of adjusting to what the International Energy Agency (IEA) called the “most severe oil supply shock in history.” Oil prices rose from just over $70 a barrel before the war to more than $125 in April but then fell back down to the $80s and $90s, where they remained until this month.
Part of what kept prices relatively stable was additional oil production outside the Gulf. The United States, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, and Guyana together added an estimated 1.4 million barrels a day. That replaced only a fraction of the missing Gulf supply, but every barrel mattered in a tightening market.
Tapping inventories helped as well. In March, the IEA’s 32 member countries authorized the release of 400 million barrels from emergency reserves, the largest coordinated drawdown in the agency’s history, and more than double the previous record of nearly 183 million barrels released in 2022 amid the war in Ukraine. Traders and refiners also drew on commercial inventories to replace some of the missing Gulf oil and allow refiners to maintain fuel production.
Demand also fell, especially in Asia. Part of the decline was the result of a consumer response to high prices. China, the world’s largest crude importer, also made a large, orchestrated adjustment that resulted in its seaborne imports’ dropping from over 11 million barrels a day before the war to just over seven million in August. Beijing drew on its 1.4 billion–barrel oil stockpile, Chinese refineries reduced the amount of crude they processed, and the government placed restrictions on fuel exports to keep more gasoline and diesel at home. China increasingly played the role of what the energy analyst Javier Blas has called a “swing importer”: by retreating from the market when prices rose, it freed barrels for other buyers and helped prevent more acute price spikes.
After the initial shock of the war, Gulf producers found ways to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and export some of their oil. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) used a pipeline connecting its inland fields to Fujairah, a city that lies past the strait. Saudi Arabia relied on its East–West pipeline, which carries crude from the country’s eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. For much of the war, the pipeline moved four to five million barrels a day, making it the most important alternative export route.
Finally, restraint among the war’s belligerents kept the level of disruption to energy markets much lower than it could have been. There were still some significant incidents. Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field in March, after which Iran carried out strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan refinery, knocking out approximately 17 percent of Qatar’s liquefied natural gas export capacity. It could take years for the site to become fully functional again. But these attacks proved to be exceptions. Although more than 80 energy facilities across the region have been hit—including Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura port, Bahrain’s Sitra refinery, several Kuwaiti refineries, and the UAE’s Habshan gas complex and Fujairah export facilities—the bulk of the region’s infrastructure survived intact and operational.
This was no accident. Iran, Israel, and the United States largely avoided sustained attacks on the region’s largest oil fields, processing plants, pipelines, and export terminals because they all had reason to hold back. Given the difficulty of defending against drones, missiles, and bombs, large-scale attacks on critical infrastructure would likely have succeeded and invited reprisals in kind, leaving everyone worse off. Washington, under pressure from concerned Arab governments that feared such escalation, refrained from carrying out the sort of massive attacks on Iran’s oil and gas facilities that Trump threatened on multiple occasions, and it pressed Israel to exhibit similar restraint. Tehran, for its part, declined to strike its neighbors’ vulnerable energy installations because it knew that its own oil and gas facilities, the last engine left powering the Iranian economy, would have met with the same fate. It was the energy equivalent of the mutual assured destruction doctrine, which brought stability to the U.S.-Soviet nuclear standoff during the Cold War.
Today, the mechanisms that contained the initial energy shock are faltering. The relative stability of energy markets was the product of several extraordinary adjustments, not a sign that the energy system can indefinitely endure a war that continues to take infrastructure offline. Countries have already used the quickest and least economically damaging tools available to stabilize oil and gas prices. Now, with easy-to-mobilize production already online, alternative transit routes already operational, and reserves running low, few good options remain at their disposal.
Oil and gas production outside the Gulf will continue to grow, but slowly. Further increases to supply would require additional drilling and investment in new pipelines and other infrastructure that would take years to develop. In the meantime, most of the world’s readily available spare production capacity is in the Gulf, yet for the foreseeable future its exporters will not have access to export routes. Another major oil producer, Russia, is unlikely to contribute much, either. The country has halted exports of most refined products, and its own energy infrastructure has come under attack in the war with Ukraine.
Further reduction in demand is also possible, but only at a mounting economic cost. China and other importing countries have already conserved fuel, reduced refinery operations, substituted other energy sources, released reserves, and absorbed higher prices. Cutting consumption of oil and gas much further would likely lead to factories closing, transportation disruptions, and a decline in overall economic activity.
Emergency inventories, meanwhile, have reached dangerously low levels and have not been replenished. These reserves are designed to bridge temporary disruptions, not replace sustained production losses. The U.S. strategic petroleum reserve has already fallen below 300 million barrels, its lowest level since the 1980s.
Most consequentially, the alternative routes that Gulf states were using to export oil have now come under attack. After drones launched from Iraq by an Iranian-aligned militia struck Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline last week, Riyadh was forced to shut it down, removing millions of barrels of oil a day—up to four percent of global supply—from the markets. Bringing it fully back online could take days, or it could take many weeks. Even if the damage can be repaired quickly, the pipeline can always be attacked again. The Houthis, moreover, have strengthened their position around the Red Sea. By mid-September, they controlled most of Yemen’s western coastline, including the strategically placed port city of Mokha and islands in and around the Bab el Mandeb Strait. The group had declared a blockade of Saudi shipping in July; now it can enforce it by threatening vessels with drones, missiles, and shorter-range weapons. Neither the Bab el Mandeb Strait nor the Strait of Hormuz is safe for tankers any longer, especially those carrying Saudi oil.
Without the means to offset another significant loss of supply, the latest escalation of the war—and any further escalation to come—risks producing an energy crisis with far-reaching consequences. Shortages of diesel, which powers trucking, agriculture, construction, industry, and much of global shipping, will spread quickly through the broader economy. Reduced liquefied natural gas supplies will pressure electricity and heating markets, particularly as Europe approaches winter with inadequate gas inventories. Fertilizer shortages will raise agricultural costs and threaten future harvests. Three-quarters of the global population live in countries that depend on energy imports. The longer these countries go without critical energy supplies, the closer their economies inch toward crisis.
The burdens will not be distributed evenly. Wealthier countries can outbid poorer ones for limited supplies. Already, many import-dependent countries face shortages, fiscal pressure, and in some cases a difficult choice between cutting fuel subsidies and risking unrest or maintaining them and further weakening public finances. Central banks everywhere are contending with elevated inflation as a result of higher energy costs, but further raising interest rates would hamper growth, especially in economies that are already struggling to cope with fuel shortages—shortages that are now driving public protests in Guatemala, Indonesia, the Philippines, Portugal, and many other countries. Especially if attacks on energy infrastructure pick up, the early fear that this regional war would produce global instability might finally become reality.
Avoiding a full-scale economic crisis requires the United States to rethink its strategy. Washington has been launching strikes on military targets and industrial infrastructure and putting economic pressure on Tehran through sanctions and a naval blockade for close to seven months now. Yet the Iranian regime shows no signs of collapsing or capitulating. Its government, dominated by hardened veterans of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and largely indifferent to the suffering of the Iranian population, appears determined to fight on. And there is good reason to think it can, relying on Russian and Chinese assistance, a trickle of oil and gas sales, and revenues stashed away early in the war when the Trump administration made the misguided decision to relieve some sanctions. For the United States and its partners, meanwhile, the economic and military costs of the war are becoming unacceptable. It is therefore time to explore diplomacy once again.
Washington should not try to merely resurrect a memorandum of understanding that it negotiated with Tehran in June. That agreement placed no constraints on groups affiliated with Iran that are now interfering with energy infrastructure, nor did it place limits on Iran’s missile and drone capabilities. It was also tilted in Iran’s favor, offering Tehran substantial economic benefits, including access to a $300 billion reconstruction fund, the termination of all sanctions, and full access to frozen assets, much of which the United States should be retaining as leverage for negotiations to limit Iran’s nuclear activities. The best way forward would be to start over, or at least to negotiate modifications to the June accord’s terms.
Whatever the starting point, renewed diplomacy should aim for a cease-fire that extends to attacks on energy infrastructure by all parties and affiliates: the United States, its Arab partners, and Israel, as well as Iran, the Houthis, and other armed groups that Tehran supports in Iraq and elsewhere. Washington should condition the cease-fire on an agreement by the Iranian regime not to alter the status of its nuclear capabilities, but at the same time signal to Tehran that a U.S. military response to any such alteration would only target nuclear facilities. Iran would also receive a to-be-negotiated degree of sanctions relief, a return of some frozen assets, and some reconstruction aid, as long as it adhered to the terms of the agreement.
Some pressure on the global energy trade would ease right away: the United States would end its blockade of Iranian vessels, and Iran would end all mining of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on tankers using its shipping lanes. Ideally, negotiators would also be able to work out a plan for a multilateral governing authority to oversee and collect reasonable fees for passage through the Strait of Hormuz. A resumption of free transit would be preferable, but some kind of fee structure has likely become unavoidable, given that the June agreement accepted Iran’s right to collect payments. The best outcome now would be a system in which all Gulf countries (including Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE) participated rather than endorsing the Iranian-Omani governance regime advocated by those two countries.
A U.S.-Iranian accord alone would not eliminate all risk to the regional energy system. Tehran probably does not hold enough sway over the relatively autonomous Houthis, for instance, to induce that group to end its military action against Saudi Arabia. Riyadh might therefore need to reach a separate cease-fire agreement with the Houthis to fully secure its energy infrastructure—a tall task, given that Saudi Arabia’s dispute with the group is tied up in Yemen’s 12-year civil war. Any deal would almost certainly need to accept the Houthis’ participation in Yemeni politics and provide the group economic benefits, possibly including a share of Yemen’s oil revenues. Washington should push Riyadh to negotiate before its conflict with the Houthis escalates further and sends the price of energy even higher—or threatens the stability of Saudi Arabia itself.
The United States would benefit from an end to all hostilities in the Gulf. Energy prices would quickly fall, relieving shortages and inflationary pressures. The danger of escalation that would destroy the region’s energy infrastructure and plunge the world into recession would diminish. Washington would be able to withdraw the bulk of its troops from the region, rebuild its munitions inventories, and begin to restore its military readiness. Iran would also have something to gain: it would no longer have to fear devastating attacks on its own energy infrastructure, and it would reap considerable economic benefits from the resumption of oil and gas sales and from collecting new transit fees—not to mention any sanctions relief, unfreezing of assets, and reconstruction aid that would be part of a deal.
Whether the benefits of a cease-fire—and the risks of continued fighting—would persuade both Tehran and Washington to come to the table is a separate question. Both have been reluctant to lay down arms without a clear victory. Iranian decision-makers, moreover, may see any new U.S. effort to end the war as evidence of American weakness and reason to stand firm. Yet the dire state of the Iranian economy, with its negative growth, high inflation, and plummeting currency, might make a diplomatic off-ramp attractive to Tehran, especially among elites who may already be worrying about the stability of their rule. To help nudge Iranian leaders’ calculations in the direction of peace, the United States should make public the terms of any agreement and point out the benefits that would accrue to Iran, with the aim of adding to the internal pressure on the regime. It should also recruit China’s help in pressing Iran to compromise—a role Beijing may be amenable to playing to reduce the chances of escalation that leads to a global economic crisis, which would harm China’s own economy, too.
articles.summary: A diplomatic strategy to end the war.

articles.title: Europe Can’t Get Out of Its Own Way
