No two UN insiders have the same recipe for boiling down this profusion of entities, although all agree that consolidation is needed—just not in their own agency. The next secretary-general will therefore need to knock heads together and streamline how the UN raises funds, organizes crisis response, and deconflicts between the mandates of its constituent parts.
Just as candidates see a case for consolidation, they also share the view that reform should center on reviving the UN’s role in peacemaking. In this they reflect the prevailing view among diplomats in New York that Guterres has too frequently neglected peace and security. In some of the major wars during his tenure, including those in Ethiopia and Sudan, he has concentrated on providing humanitarian access and stayed away from efforts to find political solutions, citing the office’s relative powerlessness.
The secretary-general’s reticence in the face of war is understandable. Splits among the Security Council members with veto powers have constrained the UN’s capacity to influence first-order political crises. Russia has used its veto in the Security Council to ensure that the UN has no political role in Ukraine. The Biden administration bristled at UN efforts to promote a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas in Gaza in late 2023, and Trump’s own cease-fire plan marginalized the UN in favor of his Board of Peace. Washington has paid scant attention to UN efforts to ease the humanitarian crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, having already blatantly disregarded the UN Charter’s prohibition on acts of aggression when it launched its war in Iran. China has quietly but effectively made it clear to member states that the UN should limit its role in Myanmar’s civil war.
Yet Guterres’s instinct to shrink away from peacemaking duties has also alienated many UN members who still believe that the UN should do more to help resolve conflicts where the veto power’s fundamental interests are not at stake. His tendency to emphasize global issues unrelated to conflict is also increasingly out of step with how many UN members assess the challenges that they face. In an era of expanding conflict, ambassadors in New York say their capitals want to know what the UN can offer in the way of security. They may value cooperation in other areas, but matters of peace and war take precedence.
The candidates vying to succeed Guterres acknowledge this reality. Despite having mainly worked on trade and development at the UN, for instance, Grynspan has said her “priority will be to restore confidence in the UN as a trusted convenor in theaters of conflict.” But it is easier to promise to be a peacemaker than to resolve actual wars, not least when countries with veto powers are involved. And even in conflicts in which permanent members of the Security Council are not directly implicated, influential middle powers can make peacemaking a major challenge: the Gulf powers have largely sidelined the organization in Sudan.
To restore faith in the UN’s core mission, the next secretary-general must show both the veto-holding powers and the organization’s wider membership that it can play a useful role in averting and ending conflicts. It can do so with strategies and tools already on hand. During the Cold War, Secretary-General U Thant mediated between the United States and the Soviet Union, making possible the backchannel diplomacy that resolved the Cuban missile crisis. Over the decades since, the UN has built up unrivaled expertise on managing mediation processes, along with logistics and administrative structures necessary to mount large-scale peace and stabilization missions. The Trump administration acknowledged as much last year, when it lobbied the Security Council to mandate that the UN backstop a Gang Suppression Force in Haiti.
Although the UN can still get large numbers of boots on the ground where necessary, the demand for large-scale multinational peace operations—the hallmark of UN crisis management in the 1990s and early 2000s—is likely to remain low. Instead, the next secretary-general should focus on quieter, cheaper forms of crisis diplomacy, devoting time and energy to shuttling between the veto-holding powers and middle powers as an impartial source of advice and ideas. This work will involve more behind-the-scenes trust building than dramatic public breakthroughs. But if the UN’s next leader can convince the world that the organization is a reliable peacemaker, it may lay the groundwork for more ambitious work in the future.
A renewed focus on peacemaking does not mean the UN must abandon all other goals entirely. The organization’s leaders will, however, need to choose their priorities wisely. In 2015, UN members agreed an ambitious set of sustainable development goals, including a promise to end extreme poverty globally by 2030. After the economic shocks associated with the COVID-19 pandemic, Ukraine, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, they have little chance of reaching them. Diplomats are preparing to negotiate a new package of goals for the period after 2030. The 2015 goals involved 169 specific targets spread across 17 policy baskets ranging from “life on land” to peace, justice, and security, the sheer complexity of which has made it harder to rally political and public support for the main points of the agenda.
Many UN members will want to keep (or even add to) this diversity of initiatives. But the next UN chief may have to call for a tighter agenda centered on poverty reduction, climate change adaptation, and buffering countries against global economic shocks. Many diplomats from developing countries fret that richer states want to dump the development agenda altogether; the Trump administration has partially confirmed their suspicions by disowning the existing development goals. Agreeing on a shorter, better-defined list of post-2030 targets could help donors and developing countries find common ground.
A similar tempering of ambition may be necessary on global challenges such as climate change and the regulation of new technologies. The UN’s current preferred method of advancing agreements on these issues tends to involve a surfeit of conferences and statements. For example, 55,000 people representing states, private companies, and civil society groups registered to attend the UN summit on climate change in Brazil last year. Although these generous invitation lists may look inclusive, they are not a recipe for clear decision-making.
The next secretary-general will need to reflect on how to initiate policy on complex global problems without all the hoopla. Diplomats recalling the practices of successful secretaries-general emphasize that they developed major policy carefully with small numbers of diplomatic allies. Just as secretary-generals’ conflict-resolution work may involve more behind-the-scenes contacts and fewer large blue helmet deployments, their diplomacy around global issues may involve more quiet gatherings and fewer megaconferences. This has downsides: the UN can use global sentiment as political fuel, especially when powerful states are wary of acting. To be sure, there will be times when the secretary-general wants to rile up global public opinion. But low-key coalition building will just as often work better.
Experts pondering the future of multilateralism often wonder what it would take to get the UN back on track. Some believe that the institution’s internal contradictions will eventually force members to agree to a full-scale review of its charter, a drastic step that could just as easily exacerbate diplomatic tensions as it could ameliorate them. Others speculate that a major shock—a catastrophic AI-enabled attack on multiple countries’ infrastructures or a cascade of climate-related disasters—could jolt governments into recognizing the need for multilateral cooperation.
The next secretary-general should quietly plan for such scenarios. If and when one occurs, the better prepared the UN is the more relevant it will be. In the meantime, the incoming UN leadership needs to regain the trust of the government and peoples it serves by showing that it can make a dent in the global rise in conflicts, focus its diplomatic and operational efforts better, and offer a platform for pragmatic global problem solving. This slimmer UN may be the UN the world needs.
articles.summary: The next secretary-general must get back to basics

articles.title: America’s Attrition Trap
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
NADIA SCHADLOW is a Senior Fellow at the Hudson Institute. In 2017, she served as U.S. Deputy National Security Adviser for Strategy in the first Trump administration.
Attrition is the defining feature of today’s conflicts. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have become grinding contests over which side can exhaust the other’s military capacity, economic resources, and political will. They all, of course, have unique characteristics, but their similar trajectories reflect a deeper change in how wars now unfold. Throughout the war in Ukraine, artillery crews have repeatedly had guns and could locate their targets but have lacked the shells to fire. Ukrainian engineers have found that new kinds of drones are met with Russian countermeasures within weeks, undercutting any advantage they briefly had. And in Iran, the United States degraded its adversary’s military and destroyed deeply buried nuclear facilities but failed to resolve the political problem that made the weapons a threat in the first place.
Each dynamic illustrates a different gap that helps explain why states increasingly choose strategies of attrition—or find themselves trapped in them. The first is between the military capacity that countries possess on paper and the power that they can actually deploy and sustain. The second is between traditional principles of warfare and a modern battlefield on which technology makes decisive breakthroughs increasingly difficult. The third is between military means and the political ends they are intended to achieve.
In combination, these mismatches push wars toward attrition. When countries cannot generate and regenerate enough military capacity to overwhelm an enemy, war becomes a test of endurance. When breakthroughs are elusive, pursuing incremental gains and the steady destruction of enemy capacity becomes attractive. And when the combatants’ political end goals are too muddy or maximalist, imposing costs indefinitely can seem like the only alternative to capitulation.
For the United States, this poses a particular challenge. As American leaders increasingly seek short, decisive military operations, the United States may increasingly confront adversaries that see advantages in prolonging conflicts. The United States may not choose attrition, but it must be prepared to fight and win wars in which its adversaries do.
Military power is traditionally measured by what countries possess—assets such as troops, weapons platforms, and munitions inventories. But recent wars have exposed the gap between nominal power and usable military capability. In his 2015 book, How the War Was Won, the historian Phillips O’Brien argued that even during World War II, winning the major battles that captured the popular imagination had actually become less important than dominating what he called the “super-battlefield,” the vast expanse of factories and supply lines over which military power is produced and transported. Since that war, the ability to generate and sustain military power has only become more important. Modern militaries consume materiel at an incredible clip, and their adversaries have become increasingly capable of disrupting the production and supply networks needed to replace it.
When Russia invaded Ukraine again in early 2022, it appeared to possess overwhelming military superiority. Days before the invasion, the chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff told lawmakers that Kyiv could fall within 72 hours of a full-scale assault; speaking to The New York Times, Ukrainian commanders said that they believed that their forces had little chance against the more than 100,000 Russian troops that had massed on their border. Yet because it could not swiftly translate its vast resources into sustained combat power at the front, Russia failed to employ its capabilities effectively and take Kyiv.
But its material and manpower reserves allowed Russia to survive its early setbacks. Russia could mobilize more personnel, draw on large ammunition stocks, increase weapons production, and turn to partners such as North Korea to sustain its fight. Russia developed a theory of victory that proposed that it did not need to defeat Ukraine decisively if it could outlast it, wearing it down while waiting for Europe’s and the United States’ political commitment to weaken. Attrition gave Russia a military advantage. It also exposed a different problem among Ukraine’s powerful NATO backers: aggregate power does not necessarily translate into the capacity to sustain a prolonged, high-consumption war.
The United States and NATO have far greater economic and military power than Russia does. Yet a war of attrition measures power differently. GDP cannot be fired from artillery tubes. Total defense spending cannot, itself, intercept missiles. The defense industries of Ukraine’s partners were not built to replace ammunition rapidly; they were organized around peacetime production. They thus struggled to convert their latent potential quickly enough into shells, interceptors, and other usable military capabilities.
Russia and NATO thus encountered the capacity gap in almost opposite ways. Russia initially had capacity without commensurate effectiveness. Ukraine’s backers had effectiveness without sufficient depth to sustain a prolonged war.
The conflict between U.S. and Israeli forces and Iran has presented a different iteration of this dynamic. Iran’s conventional military power could not match that of Israel or the United States, but Tehran had spent decades building the ability to compensate for its conventional inferiority by creating military capacity outside its territory. Iran’s network of proxies, sometimes called its “ring of fire,” allowed Tehran to apply pressure across multiple fronts, forcing Israel and the United States to expend interceptors and sustain high operational tempos. Iran’s use of inexpensive drones and missiles exposed the limitations of costly interceptors, expensive ships, and cutting-edge aircraft. In this strategy of attrition, Iran just needs to keep imposing costs and regenerating what is lost.
On the eve of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, one U.S. general admired Moscow’s “learning and adaptive force.” Ukraine proved able to adapt even more quickly. But fast adaptation by both countries produced a paradox. Advantages that might have once enabled a breakthrough became temporary; neither side could sustain an advantage long enough to produce decisive results.
This is the second gap. As technology changes battlefields, traditional principles for creating a military advantage—such as maneuvering forces and massing combat power—are becoming harder to apply, driving wars toward attrition. In an era of drones, massed forces can make them easier to detect and destroy; the concentrations of forces and logistics required for large-scale maneuver can be detected and targeted before a breakthrough can be achieved. The element of surprise is harder to create when the battlefield is under constant observation. Technological advancement constantly creates new opportunities, but counter-adaptation erases the advantages quickly.
Quick adaptation during war is, of course, not new. But what is changing is the speed at which innovative tactics and operations can be rendered ineffective. In Ukraine, the feedback loop for learning runs directly from the battlefield to engineers and manufacturers and back again. QR codes allow troops on the ground to communicate problems such as drone malfunctions directly with support teams at the drone manufacturer, which can then alter production runs quickly. Ukrainian drone makers have described R & D cycles measured in weeks: as Russian jamming and faster drones defeat existing systems, manufacturers change frequencies, airframes, and propulsion and move the modified systems toward production. As the defense strategist Can Kasapoglu observed in July, “Unmanned systems, combat data, and human command have fused into kill chains that operate at unprecedented speed,” meaning that the war in Ukraine “has evolved from a narrow contest of platforms to a battle fought at machine speed and dictated by algorithms.”
Technology is also changing how traditional principles of war are applied in the Middle East. Consider mass. Israel and the United States have used intelligence, precision weapons, and long-range strikes to mass effects without having to mass literal forces. Iran has applied the same principle differently, using large salvos of missiles and drones to overwhelm sophisticated defenses. Because both sides can persistently generate concentrated effects without concentrating forces, destroying the enemy’s ability to keep fighting becomes harder. The contest shifts toward repeated exchanges, replenishment, and endurance. In this sense, rapid adaptation can reinforce attrition.
The third and perhaps most difficult strategic gap is that the military means being deployed in the current wars are not producing the desired political outcomes. This is true in both Russia’s war against Ukraine and in the broader Middle East confrontation involving the United States, Israel, Iran, and Iran’s regional allies and proxies. In these wars, the combatants are not pursuing limited adjustments to territorial borders or modest changes in an adversary’s behavior. The wars, instead, involve ambitious objectives that are nonnegotiable. Russia refuses to accept a Ukraine that is not in its sphere of control, and Ukraine is fighting for its right to exist as an independent state. Israel faces adversaries that reject its right to exist. The United States and Israel view an Iranian nuclear weapon as a fundamental threat to the regional security balance, while Iran sees its nuclear program and regional role as central to its security and power.
Such huge stakes leave little room for compromise, making the wars deeply intractable. Attrition is inflicting high costs in blood and treasure, apparently without narrowing those political differences. As 2022 approached, Ukraine was already mired in the long-running conflict that had begun in 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea, and had largely stagnated; NATO had never made a decision to push Russia back to its pre-2014 borders. Following Russia’s invasion in 2022, Europe and the United States still did not make the expulsion of Russia from Ukrainian territory the explicit political objective, nor did they define an alternative political settlement. Instead, they often expressed their objectives as principles, such as supporting Ukrainian sovereignty and territorial integrity for “as long as it takes” and refusing to reward Russian aggression. Military strategy, however, needs to be organized around a concrete, attainable political end state to be effective.
This ambiguity was understandable: defining a concrete objective and committing the military means to achieve that objective risked putting the United States and NATO on a direct collision course with Russia. But the result has been a military strategy detached from a political strategy—a determination merely to prevent Ukraine’s defeat and impose costs on Russia indefinitely.
In the Middle East, a similar problem has emerged. Military force has imposed enormous costs on both Hamas and Iran, devastating their military facilities and killing their commanders. But it has not led either to capitulate. Early in Israel’s war against Hamas, Graham Allison and Amos Yadlin argued in Foreign Affairs that Israel had defeated Hamas because it had killed most of its military leaders and more than half of its fighters. But destroying an enemy’s military capacity is not the same as producing the political conditions required for a durable end to the conflict.
Iran has used politics—in this case, international pressure—as a tool in its war of attrition. It has sought to degrade international support for Israel, creating a political ring of fire around its adversary. Avril Haines, the United States’s director of national intelligence under President Joe Biden, disclosed in July 2024 that Iranian government-linked actors were posing as activists online, encouraging Gaza protests, and providing financial support to protesters in the United States. International institutions, many European governments, and public opinion around the world have increased pressure on Israel, and its isolation has deepened. This has had strategic consequences. Although Israel has demonstrated that it can dominate militarily, it has struggled to translate those victories into a more favorable regional political environment. Its relationships with European and other foreign governments have deteriorated, and those divisions now complicate the international discussions over postwar arrangements in Gaza.
For the United States, wars of attrition create a particular strategic dilemma. The Pentagon has planned for short, decisive military operations, and political leaders in Washington often promise them. Yet adversaries today have the means and incentives to deny the United States that kind of war and prolong conflicts in the hope that they can regenerate capacity, impose costs, and outlast American political will.
At the same time, the United States has built a military that relies heavily on relatively small numbers of sophisticated and expensive weapons systems, an industrial base that cannot rapidly replace many of these systems, and strategies that too often leave the political conditions required for victory unresolved. U.S. defense planners are making some efforts to change this military posture, but it will take time. The danger is not that the United States cannot win a war of attrition. It is that it remains organized around the expectation that it will not have to fight one.
Nearly four decades ago, the military thinker Edward Luttwak proposed a strategy of “relational maneuver,” which would focus on attacking the enemy’s internal cohesion and functioning rather than simply grinding down its forces. Recently, the Trump administration has hinted that it may be trying to adopt such a strategy in Iran. The newly launched Operation Economic Outcast aims, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it, to create an “economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe.” This broader pressure may weaken the regime or eventually cause it to collapse—if the United States finds the political will to sustain such pressure. That it will, however, cannot be assumed: rising energy prices and other economic costs will test Washington’s willingness to maintain pressure over time. The most realistic outcome in Iran may be an unresolved stalemate.
Breaking this pattern will require a change in thinking in Washington. U.S. military leaders must build forces and concepts around the assumption that future wars are unlikely to be resolved quickly, while political leaders must be more realistic about whether the objectives they set can be achieved by military force alone and in a short time frame. Such adjustments will not be easy. The more dangerous possibility is that the United States will continue to drift into attritional conflicts because their price initially appears manageable, even as the human and economic costs mount. Americans may reject the notion of “forever wars.” But U.S. adversaries have every incentive to deny the United States the short, decisive conflicts it prefers. And even wars that prove relatively easy to sustain can be very difficult to end for good.
articles.summary: The U.S. military needs to build up its endurance.

articles.title: Ebola Is Only the Beginning
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
STEPHANIE PSAKI is a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and was U.S. Coordinator for Global Health Security at the National Security Council from 2023 to 2025.
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a stunning indictment of the state of global health security. The epidemic should have been containable; few threats are as familiar to health officials and institutions as this one. Ebola viruses were first discovered in northern Congo (then Zaire) in 1976; since then, they have caused 16 outbreaks in that country and dozens more in the region. Ebola remains highly lethal, but over the past five decades, medical professionals and governments have learned how to diagnose the disease, detect its spread, and, when caught early, stop it. Yet the outbreak that has killed over 3,500 people across Congo since early this year is already the deadliest the country has experienced and the fastest spreading in history. Despite recent signs of progress, it is nowhere near being contained.
The difficulty containing this year’s Ebola outbreak does not bode well for the world’s ability to respond effectively to future biological threats. Naturally occurring viruses are emerging more frequently. There were 12 recorded outbreaks of Ebola and Marburg, another deadly disease from the same viral family, during the four years of the Biden administration, compared with five during the previous four years; the current Trump administration could well face even more, having already contended with five outbreaks in less than two years. And the risk of an accidental or deliberate release of a deadly virus is growing. A rising number of labs are handling high-risk pathogens, in part because of a research boom following the COVID-19 pandemic, and it is becoming easier and easier to engineer new viruses using artificial intelligence. Earlier this month, the American AI company Anthropic disclosed five cases in which scientists used its AI software Claude for research that could support biological weapons development, including on variants of bird flu that could evade human immunity. The report confirmed fears that AI models could help bad actors access biological weapons.
The global health system, meanwhile, has been weakened by the Trump administration’s cuts to disease surveillance and outbreak preparedness programs, both within the United States and abroad. But the system was shaky long before U.S. President Donald Trump arrived on the scene. Global threat monitoring processes have significant gaps, inconsistent funding models delay vaccine development, and most countries underinvest in regular, comprehensive health services. Washington and other donors often step up when a crisis emerges, but scrambling to put together an emergency response is far from the best way to handle a biological threat. That approach is struggling to contain Ebola today. When a new, lesser-known pathogen begins to spread, the world needs to be much better prepared.
The current outbreak in Congo likely began at least eight months ago. Residents of Mongbwalu, a small town in the northeastern part of the country, described entire families dying from a mysterious illness as early as January. The virus spread for months before the Congolese government, with help from the World Health Organization (WHO), was able to confirm the source of the outbreak in mid-May. By then, hundreds of cases had already been detected across multiple communities in Congo, and two cases had been confirmed in Uganda. Some delay in detection is to be expected, given the remote location of the earliest deaths, ongoing conflict in the area, and the rarity of this outbreak’s driver, the Bundibugyo virus. But the fact that no previous Ebola outbreak had spread as far before being detected suggests that the global health system is becoming less, not more, prepared to manage biological threats.
Four months after the outbreak was confirmed, responders from the Congolese government, the WHO, and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) are still struggling to contain it. The death rate sits at around 50 percent, much higher than in past Bundibugyo outbreaks, and 60 percent of deaths between mid-July and late August happened outside health facilities. These two patterns suggest that the true numbers of illnesses and deaths are higher than the official figures and that the disease continues to spread beyond the reach of health officials. Although there have been some signs of progress recently, WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has warned that, if the outbreak’s current trajectory continues, the death toll could exceed that of the world’s largest-ever Ebola outbreak, the epidemic that killed more than 11,000 people and infected nearly 30,000 across West Africa between 2014 and 2016.
The United States’ withdrawal from the WHO and dissolution of the U.S. Agency for International Development almost certainly weakened the capacity of both the WHO and the Congolese government to respond to the Ebola outbreak. Nicholas Enrich, a career civil servant who briefly led USAID’s global health work in the early months of the Trump administration, has described in his book Into the Wood Chipper how he tried to convince politically appointed USAID leaders to restart contracts for Ebola response efforts that were canceled amid an outbreak of the disease in Uganda that began in January 2025. Although the Trump administration has said that those programs resumed, former USAID partners, including the International Rescue Committee and Oxfam, have confirmed publicly that Washington stopped funding their health programs in eastern Congo in 2025. The Trump administration also fired most of USAID’s health security staff, eliminated a National Security Council team formed after the 2014 Ebola outbreak to focus on health security and biodefense, and left the leadership position in the congressionally mandated White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy vacant for a year. It terminated thousands of staff positions at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, including entire branches of the CDC’s Global Health Center, and prohibited the agency from communicating with the WHO. After all these cuts and restrictions, Ebola was able to circulate for four months without U.S. experts or partner organizations sounding any alarm bells.
The Trump administration has insisted its actions have not affected the detection or containment of Ebola: a White House spokesperson asserted instead, in May, that USAID cuts had made the “entire global health apparatus more efficient and responsive.” Yet it is hard to believe that closing offices, firing government staff, and terminating disease detection and response partnerships has nothing to do with the fact that this Ebola outbreak is one of the worst in history. In recent months, Washington has scrambled to close gaps created by earlier cuts, including by filling vacant roles and committing more than $500 million in assistance to the Ebola response—far more than any other country has committed. But these emergency measures become more expensive and less effective when the health systems carrying out the response have already been compromised by aid cuts.
Perhaps even more alarming than the loss of U.S. support for outbreak prevention is a set of wider failures in the global health system. Catching an outbreak in the first few days or weeks is essential to quickly containing it. But this outbreak has shown that the existing processes for detecting viruses early are insufficient. For decades, health workers have relied on tests for specific pathogens in places known to be at high risk—such as tests for Ebola in Congo or tests for hantavirus in Argentina. Such a system was always destined to fail. Health officials in northeastern Congo had Ebola tests on hand earlier this year, but the tests were not designed to pick up the Bundibugyo species. This will not be the last time an unusual strain of a disease begins to circulate. Viruses change. Infected people get on planes and travel to less monitored regions. Scaling up supplies of existing tests is not a feasible solution to these problems, either; tests are often expensive, and health workers usually need specialized training to administer them.
Once Ebola began spreading in Congo, government officials and responders from nongovernmental organizations should have been able to work closely with the communities affected by the disease. Yet distrust and fear have led to hundreds of attacks on health workers and facilities and have generally made it difficult for response teams to identify those who have been infected and take steps to prevent further spread. These obstacles are not surprising. Millions of people across Congo were already dealing with malaria, measles, and malnutrition; more than 20,000 people died of malaria in 2024 alone. But only when Ebola, a disease with the potential to spread around the world, reaches their communities do resources start pouring in from high-income countries and multilateral institutions. People are naturally skeptical of international efforts to contain one emergency when the same global health system is not addressing the other crises they are suffering through. This relative lack of attention to other diseases creates practical problems, too: because the early symptoms of Ebola, such as fever, resemble those of other common illnesses, many people avoid seeking care until they are very sick, increasing their chances of death and the likelihood that they will transmit the virus.
Regional insecurity has also hindered efforts to detect and contain the outbreak. Eastern Congo has been embroiled in conflict for decades, and fighting along the Ugandan and Rwandan borders has worsened in the last few years. An estimated nine million Congolese people have been displaced, many of them having fled to neighboring countries or to overcrowded camps that lack water, sanitation, and basic health services. These camps are already struggling with high levels of malaria, measles, and cholera, and there is a growing risk that Ebola will begin to circulate inside them, too. Meanwhile, violence in the area endangers public health workers and makes it difficult to transport supplies to northeastern Congo. Political leaders are aware that the conflict is slowing progress in the Ebola response. But until they can find a path to peace, health systems need more effective tools for operating in conflict settings, including finding easier ways to transport supplies, creating stockpiles of personal protective equipment for health workers, building stronger partnerships with trusted local leaders who can help spread accurate information, and maintaining functioning health, water, and sanitation infrastructure for displaced communities.
Perhaps the most promising element of the Ebola response has been the relatively quick development of vaccines for the Bundibugyo virus. The first vaccine dose was administered in a Phase 1 trial within 12 weeks of the outbreak’s confirmation, half the time it took researchers to reach the same stage during the 2014 Ebola crisis. In part, this speed was facilitated by long-term U.S. and European investments in institutions such as the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), a public-private partnership, and the government-run Uganda Virus Research Institute. These and other organizations had collected key materials, built laboratories, and cultivated scientific partnerships in advance so that they were ready to be used in an emergency.
Fast as this development process has been, however, it will take months before any of the new vaccine candidates could be used to inoculate the broader public. For now, containment efforts remain fully dependent on public health measures such as contact tracing and isolation, which require a large, well-coordinated response team. Vaccine development needs to move more quickly, but the current system is not designed to make that happen. Too often, funding emerges only after a crisis is underway. Scientists had the capacity to develop and begin testing vaccines and treatments for Bundibugyo virus before the current outbreak; what they did not have was money and political support.
The latest Ebola outbreak has exposed serious gaps in the world’s capacity to respond to the most predictable of health emergencies. The next threat could be far more complex. Last month, a paper in Science confirmed the first-ever successful synthesis of a complete, functional viral genome using AI. This month, Anthropic confirmed that scientists in several countries are using its AI models in ways that could cause widespread harm. In the very near future, bad actors may be able to use AI to engineer viruses at home that are intentionally designed to evade human immunity and existing countermeasures.
The current crisis should serve as a wake-up call, just as the Ebola outbreak in West Africa did a decade ago. That epidemic spurred the United States and many other countries to invest in new research and development, which resulted in an Ebola vaccine that has since been used to save lives and contain multiple outbreaks. It pushed the U.S. government to create new processes for responding to biothreats and build 13 units on American soil where medical staff can safely care for people infected with Ebola and other highly deadly diseases. And it prompted the African Union to launch the Africa CDC in 2017, improving the continent’s ability to manage regional outbreaks.
Today, governments, together with the private sector and multilateral institutions, have a similar opportunity to strengthen global health security. Part of the solution lies in innovation. Some of the same technological advances that are increasing the risk of bioweapons make it possible for the United States and other countries to establish national systems to quickly detect known and unknown biological threats and to rapidly develop tests, treatments, and vaccines when threats emerge. The U.S. government has the financial capacity and the incentives to develop such a system within the next few years and deploy it domestically. Ideally, it would then be extended globally. There would need to be some international agreement about how to pay for the system so that critical countries such as Congo could participate, however, and a few countries, including China, which has refused to share complete information about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic, may be reluctant to join. Yet even an early warning system that covers most but not all of the globe would be an improvement on the monitoring processes currently in place.
Vaccine development also requires greater investment and political commitment. Institutions such as CEPI are already working to change the current model, which forces scientists to scramble after a health crisis is already underway, by pursuing research on medical countermeasures for entire viral families that can easily be adapted when one particular virus causes an outbreak. But they need time and additional funding. The World Bank and the WHO have estimated that about $10.5 billion in international financing would be needed annually for a full global pandemic preparedness and response system, roughly $2 billion of which would be focused on research and access to vaccines, treatments, and supplies. It’s a large sum, but it’s cheaper than allowing a deadly disease to spread; the COVID-19 pandemic cost the U.S. economy alone an estimated $14 trillion. Governments will need to lead cross-border collaboration on rapid information sharing, plans to manufacture and distribute vaccines and other medical products, and streamlining regulatory and legal systems. But they should also seek partnerships with AI companies, whose technological expertise can help speed up the development of more broadly protective vaccines.
Finally, roles need to be more clearly divided among local, regional, and multilateral health institutions. National governments, in partnership with outside actors when needed, must ensure that communities are protected from known threats such as malaria and measles. Africa CDC and other regional institutions, which are more accountable to national governments than global institutions are, should be tasked with building cross-border surveillance and communication systems. And at the multilateral level, the WHO must focus on its core mandate of offering technical guidance on cross-border health threats and helping coordinate outbreak responses rather than submitting to pressure from member states to spread its limited staff and budget across too many health issues.
The current ad hoc system relies too heavily on the United States to mobilize people and resources to respond to each new emergency. It has struggled to contain Ebola. And it will struggle even more when a far less familiar pathogen causes an outbreak. Governments need to build a better global health infrastructure before that day arrives.
articles.summary: Congo’s warning for the global health system.

articles.title: Cuba’s Point of No Return
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
WILL FREEMAN is Fellow for Latin America Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.
In central Havana, a giant mound of sand-colored rubble fills an entire city block. It is all that remains of the Superior Institute of Industrial Design—a stately building that in its 166 years housed a Spanish officers’ club, U.S. occupation forces after 1898, Cuba’s health ministry, and, finally, the design school. Declared uninhabitable years ago, it suffered two partial collapses in 2025. The state never sent anyone to fix it. This past February, what remained suddenly fell, entombing several squatters. When I visited in June, skinny men scaled the craggy surface, prying loose bits of brick that they carted off to build makeshift houses.
Cuba, on its current trajectory, is headed for the fate of the design school: what lies ahead is an accelerating collapse of the state and economy. Unless this course is reversed soon, rebuilding the island as a stable, prosperous, and democratic place could become virtually impossible.
A few months ago, a slow unraveling was not what most observers expected. Because of the tariff threat in place since February against countries supplying oil to Cuba, President Donald Trump’s warnings of military action, and reports of secret talks between Havana and Washington, many believed that either a power-sharing deal or a Venezuela-style military operation was imminent.
By late May, that looked less likely. By then, according to the Miami Herald, the backchannel talks had collapsed amid opposition from Florida Republicans and Havana’s rejection of Washington’s offer: U.S. investment and petroleum in exchange for President Miguel Díaz-Canel’s removal and the privatization of Cuba’s state oil company. Havana enacted 176 economic reforms in June, which expanded space for the private sector, but this did not satisfy Washington. While allowing limited U.S. fuel and food to reach the island through private distributors, the Trump administration added new sanctions against state companies and regime officials. In August, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Axios that the policy’s timeline had shifted, saying that it would take “patience and persistence” and that the regime could survive into 2028 or beyond.
There are a few ways to read Rubio’s comments. One is that the administration is bluffing. It is threatening to maintain the current extraordinary sanctions pressure either to restart the stalled negotiations or to misdirect the regime ahead of a military operation. Another is that, with the United States entangled in Iran and busy managing Venezuela, Cuba has simply been demoted as a priority. The administration has put the island on life support, with just enough U.S. fuel and food allowed to reach private firms to prevent societal breakdown, but otherwise it has no new plan. Cuba policy has been set to autopilot. A third is that the administration has concluded that waiting for the one-party system to implode from within is the only viable path to regime change, even if it is long, tortuous, and uncertain.
Regardless, what is not widely appreciated outside Cuba is how economic and state collapse—triggered by the regime’s unwillingness to reform and hastened by U.S. sanctions—is already remaking the island. The state, aside from its capacity for political repression, is rapidly weakening. The economy is contracting and growing more unequal, leaving a large underclass too poor to participate meaningfully in the new private sector. Social cohesion is fraying, and crime is rising, while plunging birth rates and emigration warp Cuba’s demographics.
All these trends predate the foreign oil cutoff and the newest sanctions by years, if not decades, but each now appears to be accelerating. The danger is that the longer the impasse lasts, the more they will calcify into the baseline conditions for any future transition, narrowing the chances that Cuba ever becomes a well-governed country—and increasing the likelihood of an even more dysfunctional, chaotic future instead. If nothing changes soon, a transitional government could one day find itself in the same impossible position as the men atop the ruins of the design institute: trying to build something safe, habitable, and lasting out of rubble.
In Havana, I heard a joke. “Only two things work in this country: the state security apparatus and the hospitals.” It was too generous to the hospitals. About state security, it was true. Repression is the only thing the Cuban state still does well. This owes less to any apparent abundance of resources than to the leadership’s entirely rational unity. The headquarters of the Directorate of Penal Institutions, which administers the country’s prison system, is as decrepit as any building in central Havana, with cardboard filling broken windows. But the generals and spy chiefs know how much they would lose from political liberalization. If the Trump administration has tried to convince some of them that there are off-ramps, it does not appear to have succeeded. So they stick together, and the state’s capacity for repression remains intact.
Although Cubans I met were astonishingly willing to criticize the regime on street corners or within earshot of neighbors, and almost all did, none said that they would join a public protest, a near-certain route to detention. In case anyone forgot, police cars sat parked outside the family homes of detained protest leaders as ominous reminders; with fuel so scarce, it is telling that the regime can still find the gasoline to dispatch them.
On every other dimension, however, the Cuban state is weaker than most foreign observers realize—both those on the right, who imagine an anti-American leviathan, and those on the left, who cling to the fiction of functional schools and hospitals. A better description came from a European diplomat in Havana: “authoritarian anarchy,” a state that can still stifle political expression but is increasingly unable to provide public services or to prevent disorder.
Take public health, long one of the Cuban state’s proudest achievements. Access to the best clinics always depended on connections. But through the early 2010s, Cuba’s population-level health indicators, underpinned by well-trained doctors and generous public investment, were among Latin America’s strongest. Today, most hospitals lack essential supplies and medicines, forcing patients to buy everything from antibiotics to amputation saws on the black market. Although many doctors do their best under the circumstances, unlivable public salaries have made bribe-taking increasingly common. Graduating medical students pursue unrelated work in the emerging private sector or emigrate. The results are stark: infant mortality, once among the lowest in the region, has more than doubled since 2018, and mosquito-borne illnesses that the state had previously contained are back. Chikungunya alone infected up to a third of the population in 2025; cases of dengue and Zika have also surged.
Violent crime, once almost unknown on the island, is rising sharply—another sign of the state’s haphazard retreat. Although the lack of reliable official statistics makes this hard to confirm, and although Cuba still endures far less violence than several of its neighbors, fear of robbery and assault has altered many Cubans’ daily routines. Residents of Cárdenas, a small city two hours east of Havana, stay off the streets at night. Vigilantes are allegedly behind a growing number of killings of criminal suspects there and in the city of Guantánamo (not to be confused with the nearby U.S. military base of the same name).
In Havana, stories of break-ins to steal solar panels and water tanks have become common, and there is a widespread perception that police are ever more absent or bribable. Although crime is disorganized for now—driven by abject need or addiction to the cheap synthetic cannabinoid known as el químico, now everywhere on the island—it could easily cohere into something more organized.
Crumbling power plants, a shortened school year, the holes Havana residents have cut into the streets to siphon off scarce public water for resale or private consumption—the hollowing of the state is visible everywhere. The long-term effects of the embargo are partly to blame, as is the cutoff of foreign oil since February. But no one forced Cuba’s leaders to devote, by 2024, 37 times as much public capital investment to tourism, real estate, and hospitality as to health and education. That was a profit-seeking gamble by a small clique of insiders, and it failed. The question now is whether the state will be able to do anything at all, including maintain public order, after several more years of breakdown.
The second transformation remaking Cuba, and creating dilemmas for a future transition, is economic. The economy is shrinking: it has contracted by at least 15 percent since 2020, as tourism cratered and foreign investors fled for fear of new U.S. secondary sanctions. In response, the regime has grudgingly opened space for private enterprise—not because most officials favor markets but because they have concluded that some market activity is the only way to keep the island from starving or rebelling. Since the 2021 legalization of micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises, known in Spanish as MIPYMEs, these firms have come to number more than 10,000, accounting for an estimated 65 percent of all retail sales and 40 percent of total employment. June’s reforms formally expanded what private activity is permitted, although U.S. sanctions, the regime’s lack of credibility with domestic and foreign investors, and its internal divisions will likely limit their implementation.
The growth of the private sector has been positive and necessary, keeping at least some shelves stocked amid the crisis and making at least part of the population less beholden to public salaries, a source of leverage for the regime. The 2021 currency unification was another necessary step. Despite its disastrous implementation, which shredded most Cubans’ purchasing power, it ended a dual-currency system that had distorted prices and masked state enterprises’ underperformance.
But the specific way markets are taking root—with much of the population too poor to participate meaningfully, with no rule of law, and with the gap between winners and losers steadily widening—is pernicious for the country’s future. Several Cubans I met said they felt as if they were living through Russia’s 1990s: a period of murky deals and rigged competition that led not to broad-based prosperity but to oligarchs and mass immiseration. The word they repeated most was reparto—a divvying up of the country. Regime insiders are positioned to gain the most, and MIPYME owners have a foot in the door. Meanwhile, the young, the old, public-sector workers, and many Afro-Cubans are increasingly struggling just to eat. As one Cuban woman put it to me, “We took the longest, most painful road to Latin American capitalism.”
Cuba is reproducing the worst defects of certain Central American economies—rigid class differences, cronyism, remittance dependence, and low productivity—only without their comparatively stronger growth. The widening inequality is hard to miss: even now, with blackouts regularly stretching two to three days, better-off neighborhoods have new restaurants with generators humming, lights on, live DJs, and full tables. Around them stand darkened houses, and uncollected trash piles up on the street. It didn’t have to be this way. Cuba’s population remains highly educated, even as the wages MIPYMEs can pay pull skilled professionals away from their fields. A transition today could still put a dynamic and fair market economy within reach. In two or three more years, it might not.
The last dimension of Cuba’s collapse is the hardest to measure, but the one many Cubans told me they worry about most: what several described as “social decay.” The interlocking effects of mass emigration, rapid aging, and a growing generational divide pose enormous challenges for Cuba’s future.
Since 2020, Cuba’s population has fallen by an estimated 13 to 24 percent, driven largely by an unprecedented emigration wave. Because those who left were disproportionately women of reproductive age, Cuba’s already rapid aging has accelerated. By 2050, authorities forecast, one in three Cubans will be over the age of 60, up from one in four today. That would be a significant challenge even for a country with a strong economy and a functional pension system. For Cuba, it could become an insurmountable one.
Emigration has also hollowed out entire professions, emptying hospitals of health workers, schools of teachers, and even churches of priests and pastors, on a scale that Cubans have never seen before. Several middle-aged Cubans drew a contrast with the 1990s Special Period, when the loss of Soviet aid and trade shrank the economy by about 35 percent but far fewer doctors and teachers left. The island was broke then, yet hospitals and schools kept functioning. That is no longer the case. A divide has also grown between Cubans who have family abroad (and remittances with which to start businesses) and those with no such connections, disproportionately Afro-Cubans.
Living without sufficient food, energy, or medicine is exacting a psychological toll as well. The young are paying the highest price, especially those whose parents are abroad and who are growing up hungrier and more excluded than earlier generations. But the cost is generalized. “This is not resilience,” a man told me in Havana, referring to the cliché that Cubans are uniquely gifted at enduring hardship. “People can adapt to anything. We transform ourselves to manage to survive this process, but it is a degradation.”
When Cuba’s Caribbean and Central American neighbors began their transitions to democracy 40 to 50 years ago, few expected them to succeed. Most were far poorer, more economically dysfunctional, and more unequal than they are today. And yet they proved that unfavorable starting conditions are not destiny: most democratized and saw their economies grow and stabilize. Cuba could, too.
But the longer the current stalemate lasts, the dimmer that prospect grows. Sustaining the current level of pressure may cause the regime to implode, or it may not. What it will certainly do, if it persists for another year or more, is make Cuba increasingly ungovernable—by anyone.
The Trump administration may not have weighed that danger or may have judged it an acceptable cost of forcing a political opening. Strikingly, some ordinary Cubans have made the same calculation. Many I met did not believe that U.S. sanctions were primarily to blame for the current crisis. To them, whether sanctions stayed or went mattered far less than whether the regime did, since in their view it bore greater responsibility for the ruined economy. A new survey by AmericasBarometer shows something similar: 74 percent of respondents blamed the Cuban government for the current crisis, while just 16 percent blamed the United States.
All this said, the risks of sustaining the current pressure indefinitely are immense. For both countries, arguably nothing would be worse than a spiral into criminal violence and chaotic ungovernability on the island. Prolonged maximum pressure also raises the price of eventual repair, and a post-transition Cuba will have limited means of financing reconstruction. Rebuilding Cuba’s electric grid alone, degraded further with each additional blackout, will cost an estimated $8 billion. It might take the country years to regain access to financing from the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and other multilateral institutions. Given the U.S. public’s fatigue with nation building abroad, Congress is unlikely to step in to fill the gap in the meantime.
The opposite course carries costs of its own. Those who propose normalization and the lifting of the embargo without meaningful political change need to be honest about what this means: accepting that Cubans, against their will, would go on living under a regime that enriches itself while keeping citizens poor enough to control. They should have no illusions that Cuba’s leaders, with fewer sanctions, will be able to rebuild state institutions, lower inequality, or restore social cohesion. The leadership’s objective is to remain in power.
A third way may still be possible: a new offer of targeted sanctions relief, focused on alleviating the humanitarian crisis, in exchange for specific political and economic reforms that could weaken the regime’s control. Even if Havana has rejected such deals before, it is worth attempting. But whatever path Washington chooses, it must consider the costs of delay—already high and only rising.
articles.summary: The country is collapsing even as its regime survives.

articles.title: China’s Purges Are Working as Designed
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ANDREW MERTHA is George and Sadie Hyman Professor of China Studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.
For two decades, scholars believed that the main reason Chinese communist rule endured into the twenty-first century—whereas every communist regime in Europe collapsed—was that it had built sturdy, long-lasting institutions. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had moved away from the unpredictable personalist dictatorship of the Mao Zedong era and established the foundations of a modern state. It set term limits on its leaders, embraced collective leadership, and increasingly promoted officials based on merit, which made it resilient enough to bounce back from the external and internal shocks that had felled other socialist systems.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping, however, has spent the past decade demolishing nearly every institution that supposedly kept the party strong. He abolished presidential term limits in 2018, hollowed out collective leadership, and has declined to designate a successor. Xi has also purged high-level officials at will, especially in the most sensitive domain: the military. In January, only months after party leaders expelled nine senior military officers, the country’s Ministry of National Defense announced that General Zhang Youxia and General Liu Zhenli—until that point the People’s Liberation Army’s most senior uniformed officer and top operational commander, respectively—had been placed under investigation. Since 2022, according to data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the party has formally purged three dozen generals and lieutenant generals, and many more are conspicuously missing.
In Washington, many observers see these purges as evidence of China’s weakness. They see a powerful leader consumed by suspicion and obsessed with maintaining his own grip on power. If the party’s strength were indeed based on the freestanding institutions that China had built in the post-Mao era, then Xi’s purges would be a warning sign of fragility and even a potential crackup. But the party has not shown any signs of falling apart. If anything, as these purges have continued, Xi and the party appear to have only gotten stronger.
Far from weakening its rule, the way the CCP cleans its ranks can explain part of what makes it durable. A purge is not an event but a process—one that the party has run in nearly identical form for a century. It regularly targets, evaluates, and forces cadres to seek clemency to retain their standing within the system. The goal is to reform them rather than get rid of them entirely, which strengthens the party by encouraging obedience and dedication to the party’s cause. CCP leaders believe it’s working, too: Xi has embraced “self-revolution,” or continuous and permanent rectification, as the means by which China will escape the unhappy fate of the Soviet Union and other socialist regimes now residing in the dustbin of history. What could threaten the party’s longevity, then, is not the count of how many officials have been purged but the one problem that such a strategy cannot solve and can even make worse: how to handle succession. A regime of self-revolution will rise and fall on that question, no matter how hard it tries to avoid internal decay.
China’s history of purges predates the founding of the People’s Republic, in 1949. In some cases, as has been true in similar regimes, the CCP launches violent purges to remove cadres from its ranks. The type of purge now synonymous with the actions of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union aims at eliminating someone from the party, whether through incarceration, exile, or death. The victim of such a purge does not come back. Mao employed this tactic as early as 1930, when he executed more than 700 army officers in a show of total control.
But what the CCP has also done, and what is unique to its continued rule, is not a purge in the traditional sense. CCP leaders often turn to a different method of discipline: rectification. Rectification aims to keep a person inside the party, even if sometimes at a greatly diminished status. Whereas the traditional idea of a purge seeks to eliminate enemies in the ranks (the Chinese term qingdang means to “cleanse the party”), rectification aims to retain and remold cadres while keeping them in the party’s orbit.
Throughout its history, the CCP has sought to rectify cadres far more frequently than it has sought to eliminate them. In December 1929, in the village of Gutian, in Fujian province, Mao put forward a resolution called “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party” that asserted the party’s control of the military. The resolution also included clues as to how the party understood internal discipline: it described its targets not as enemies but as people who had deviations in their thinking. Cadres might suffer from ailments such as having a “purely military viewpoint” (a perspective untethered from politics), promoting ultrademocracy (a political system lacking party authority), and supporting individualism. Mao’s resolution treated each of these as a sickness that could sometimes be cured through a regimen of criticism and self-criticism in front of peers. And it attached a promise to the cure: if party members submitted to the process, the CCP would retain them rather than destroy them.
In the northern Chinese area of Yan’an, where Mao and his followers set up a wartime base camp starting in the mid-1930s, leaders turned rectification into doctrine. Party membership exploded from roughly 40,000 in 1937 to 800,000 by 1940, which meant that almost everyone in the organization was new and not yet trustworthy in the eyes of party leaders. The Rectification Movement of 1942–45 was the solution. Every cadre wrote an autobiography, measured his or her life against printed self-examination outlines, confessed before his or her party branch or work unit, and was examined, graded, and sorted by the party’s personnel department. In February 1942, Mao summarized the approach in a famous line: “Cure the sickness, save the patient.”
None of this was gentle. The Yan’an campaign was brutal: many were tortured, and thousands died. Subsequent campaigns were often even harsher. But Mao’s approach separated Chinese communism from its nearest relatives. Stalin quickly executed unreliable cadres, and Pol Pot sent them to mass graves. In China, in many cases, the strategy was to keep cadres and try to remold them while also building permanent files detailing their every mistake.
The basic procedure remains nearly identical today. A person is singled out for deviating in some way and made to write an account of his or her shortcomings. The account is checked against what his colleagues say about him and against what the organization’s records (in that individual’s personal file) already hold. The cadre is placed on a graded scale of possible sanctions, ranging from no action at one end to expulsion from the party at the other. (Most sanctions fall in the middle, including issuing a serious warning or putting someone on probation.) When a verdict on how to deal with a cadre, official, or campaign target is issued, that person, if deemed to have confessed sufficiently, is kept in the party but on terms that are revocable and conditional on the political winds. And every piece of paper the process generates goes into the cadre’s official file, permanently.
It is the process used in 1952 against a village storekeeper who skimmed off the top of procured grain. It is also the process used today for China’s Politburo, whose members—the country’s most powerful men—read self-criticisms aloud to one another once a year and have their confessions written down and permanently attached to their files following the same template that was used in Yan’an. Even as Xi has expanded the scope of who can be targeted, the machinery has not changed.
The ongoing case of the purged military officers under Xi likely fits this model, too. Zhang and Liu have been placed under investigation, not shot, and there is a chance that they remain on the party’s books, even if they are saddled with a thicker personal dossier and given a meaningless post or sidelined from public life altogether. In 2023, the diplomat Qin Gang, for instance, was removed from his position as foreign minister; news investigations reported that he had kept his party membership but had been reassigned to a low-level desk job at the foreign ministry’s publishing house. And even if Zhang and Liu are expelled from the party, purging remains the exception rather than the norm, as has been the party’s long-standing practice. Of the 101 generals and lieutenant generals that the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified as purged or potentially purged, only 14 had been officially kicked out of the party as of February.
Rectification rarely, if ever, changes cadres’ beliefs. Eighty years of evidence, much of it the party’s own, shows cadres parroting the scripts given to them, performing the required contrition, and then reverting to their earlier behaviors the moment the campaign ends. It is a process so ritualized that participants learn to say exactly what examiners want to hear.
Yet the main goal of the process is not to reform belief but to create a document to put into a dossier on file. Such a file contains objective personnel data as well as observable assessments of a cadre’s political shortcomings. It is this paper trail that enables the regime to maintain discipline even if no cadres change how they act or think.
For cadres and others subject to rectification, the process sorts who is in and who has fallen out of the good graces of party leaders. As cadres constantly jockey for status, a purge is exceptional and devastating. For most party members, surviving a rectification process with minimal punishment is grounds for relief (and often accompanied by a desire to recommit to a forgiving regime) combined with a sliver of fear that the next campaign is always just around the corner. Expanded to 100 million party members, this process produces an internalized discipline in each person that strengthens the organization’s grip on power. Each cadre wakes up every day knowing the dossier exists and that it can be used against them at any time.
The permanent, standardized, reopenable record of every party member’s history, associations, and vulnerabilities is also an information system that gives party leaders immense power. Autocratic rulers need information to head off threats to their power; the CCP’s personnel file system, filled with information about the party’s cadres, is an irreplaceable channel of information for China’s rulers. Most cadres are willing to go along with the party’s wishes, but for the small minority that does not express the proper attitude in the face of a discipline campaign, the party can expel them or put them in jail, heading off any threat of revolt from within. High-level defection and dissent sometimes occur, but when they do they are rarely organized and quickly fizzle out.
Such record-keeping might be expected to generate resentment among party cadres, but the process is designed to spread the blame and thus insulate Beijing from any backlash. There is no single person or entity that issues a rectification verdict. Instead, party task forces (known as work teams) are mobilized to draft the verdict, colleagues from their workplace endorse it, and then a committee at a higher level of administration ratifies it. It passes through enough hands in the process that authorship is aggregated and spread so that no individual leader or party entity can be said to be responsible. Even the cadre, through his or her own self-criticism, is a co-author in the verdict.
Disciplining cadres with rectification is also a coordination device. The Chinese party-state is a sprawling network of bureaucratic agencies, regional power bases, and administrative offices that have their own interests and frequently have to bargain with one another. A rectification campaign is one of the few instruments that transcends these fissures. As with the party’s other massive campaigns, such as the one-child policy, cadres understand that compliance with rectification is mandatory and a high priority for leaders. Discipline campaigns offer unambiguous carrots and sticks, including leniency for cadres who show the right attitude and professional purgatory, even exile, for those who do not. Many cadres who normally benefit from taking advantage of the fragmentation in China’s political system know to drop everything else and go along with discipline campaigns, providing Beijing with a highly visible way to impose unified priorities and strengthen party control.
Chinese history is rife with examples of once powerful dynasties weakening and eventually falling apart. To avoid this outcome, Mao’s solution was mass mobilization: only by letting the people supervise the government, he believed, would it not slacken. Xi’s answer, offered in 2021 and elaborated since, is the party’s self-revolution. In this framework, the cure for the party’s ills can only come from inside the party, not from any external force. Ongoing party rectification campaigns require all officials to discipline themselves, and the occasional outright purge of some cadres provides undeniable proof that failure to comply has consequences. It is the first time the party has explicitly located the mechanism of its own survival inside itself.
The choreography has been equally explicit. In the fall of 2014, with investigations that felled two senior military leaders underway, Xi summoned some 400 senior officers to the same hall in the village of Gutian where Mao had issued “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party.” State media called it the “new Gutian conference.” In 2024, Xi convened the military to discuss political work (that is, ideological loyalty) at Yan’an—a clear reminder that the party sees a direct line from past rectification campaigns to its present strength.
Beneath the symbolism is Xi’s fear that China could end up like the Soviet Union, whose own Communist Party, Xi believes, let its internal disciplinary mechanisms atrophy and thus was the architect of its own demise. Beijing believes that the purges and rectification must continue permanently if the party is to remain in power. Whether or not the analysis of Soviet collapse is accurate, the CCP’s continued strength suggests that the party’s method of disciplining cadres may indeed explain its durability. Xi’s purges should not be measured by how many cadres they ensnared but whether they continue to produce files, verdicts, and party retention that keep the party firmly in control.
But what strengthens the party also weakens some of China’s instruments of power. Senior military commands sit vacant or are staffed by less experienced officers, and future officers learn that the safest career record is a thin one. When forced to choose, political control is always more important to the party than operational effectiveness. This is a tradeoff that the party has been willing to make for a century and will continue to make.
And China’s method of purges cannot solve the danger of succession. Rectification produces no mechanism for choosing the next ruler—if anything, by ensuring that no subordinate accumulates independent standing, it makes the emergence of a credible successor even harder. Succession, not discipline, is where the system is weak. The older generation of CCP leaders, including Mao and Deng Xiaoping, overcame the challenge of succession by drawing on their unassailable authority as revolutionaries who had fought for the party’s survival, and subsequent leaders relied on the institutions—term limits, collective leadership, and regularized succession rules—that Xi has summarily destroyed. Xi has neither, which makes the succession problem especially acute. The moment to worry about Chinese stability is not when generals disappear amid an investigation, but when the man who reads their files begins to age out of the role without an answer as to who will follow.
The CCP is not going to collapse: the file system exists precisely to prevent elite fracture, and it has worked. What is likely to emerge instead is a state that is militarily weaker and politically stronger than most assessments suggest. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. Beijing’s own theorists are watching this, too, because they know that even a well-engineered system of rectification that has kept the party strong for a century has no answer for an elite power struggle over who comes next.
articles.summary: A unique discipline system has helped the party endure.

articles.title: Trump and Xi Can’t Stop the U.S.-China Spiral
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
Orville Schell is Arthur Ross Director of the Center on U.S.-China Relations at the Asia Society and former Dean of the Graduate School of Journalism at the University of California, Berkeley.
The United States’ epic twentieth-century successes in diplomacy set dangerously high expectations. Germany and Japan surrendered unconditionally in 1945; U.S. President Harry Truman created NATO in 1949; President John F. Kennedy resolved the Cuban missile crisis in 1962 through secret diplomatic exchanges with the Soviet premier; and in the 1980s, President Ronald Reagan, with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, negotiated landmark arms-control agreements to wind down the Cold War. Such victories accustomed many Americans to imagining that their skilled leaders could break seemingly intractable political deadlocks in decisive ways.
This hope runs especially deep in China watchers. Their sense of how diplomacy between the United States and China can unfold at its best was shaped by that game-changing moment in 1972 when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, redrew the world’s geopolitical map in the course of a weeklong visit with Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai, transforming the Cold War from a largely bipolar contest into a triangular one. Then, in 1979, U.S. President Jimmy Carter threw the door open to China in a theatrical way by welcoming the country’s paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, to the White House and restoring formal diplomatic relations with Beijing.
Today, as U.S.-Chinese relations spiral into an ever more adversarial state, the longing for another breakthrough delivered by “great men” is especially acute. U.S. President Donald Trump has egged on that desire by boastfully insisting that he alone can cut the kinds of deals the United States needs through force of personality. Even seasoned foreign policy hands who consider themselves realistic have been prone to entertaining unrealistic visions of success. When a Beijing summit between Trump and Xi was announced for the spring of 2026, the meeting was sanguinely billed in Foreign Affairs as “a geopolitical heavyweight matchup” that could “change the course of U.S.-China competition.”
Sadly, no such breakthrough came to pass. The May summit in Beijing, which I attended as a member of the press corps for this magazine, may have helped sustain a cryptic peace—a “constructive strategic stability,” as Xi euphemistically termed it. But it did not change the fundamentally adversarial nature of the relationship between the two countries. They remain locked in a dynamic of strategic ambiguity marked by endless bouts of punitive “chokehold” diplomacy, with each exploiting its control over critical supply chains to pressure the other.
Now, another Trump-Xi summit is scheduled to begin in Washington on September 23, and yearnings for a conclusive breakthrough are resurfacing. They should be tempered. The same limitations that crimped the May summit will constrain the upcoming one. The problem is not simply that the United States and China have different ideologies and political systems. It is also that neither of their leaders is suited to the kind of bargaining their current rivalry demands. Xi equates compromise with weakness and has a hard time understanding the give-a-little-to-get-a-little logic that is the heart and soul of diplomacy.
